title: Emergency Fund
text:
What it is: cash set aside for the unexpected so you never reach for credit; the target is 3 to 6 months of essential expenses, and it is Step 4 of the Financial Order of Operations
Why it matters: most derailments start with one surprise bill charged at 20 to 24% interest; Housel frames the fund as buying options, not earning a return
Essential expenses baseline: housing, groceries, utilities, transportation, health, and minimum debt payments; dining out and subscriptions do not count
Adjusting for risk: stable income with good coverage needs 3 to 4 months; dependents need 6 minimum; variable or self-employed income leans toward 6 to 9
Starter fund first: build $1,000, clear high-interest debt, then fill the full 3 to 6 month fund
Where to keep it: a high-yield savings account, money market fund, or insured credit union; not checking, stocks, long-term CDs, or cash at home
Why not the stock market: job losses and market drops tend to arrive together; Felix treats the fund as a hedge on human capital
Building it: 12 to 24 months is typical; doubling the contribution roughly halves the time; automate a payday transfer and find money in small cuts
Rebuilding: a withdrawal is the fund doing its job; resume contributions immediately without pausing retirement savings
Emergency fund math: target amount, months to reach the target, contribution needed by a deadline, and what the fund earns while you build it

title: Emergency Fund
text:
2 Your Target Amount
Your target is your essential monthly expenses multiplied by the number of months you want to cover. Each extra month adds one more block of expenses.
Formula: Target = Monthly Essential Expenses × Months of Coverage
Book example: $3,500/month in essential expenses × 4 months = $14,000. The 3 and 6 month targets are $10,500 and $21,000.





Emergency fund target at $3,500/month essential expenses







Emergency fund target at $3,500/month essential expenses





RPythonExcel


emergency_fund_target() multiplies essential monthly expenses by the months you want covered.


show/hide
emergency_fund_target <- function(monthly_expenses, months = 3) {
  monthly_expenses * months
}

emergency_fund_target(monthly_expenses = 3500, months = 3)
#> [1] 10500
emergency_fund_target(monthly_expenses = 3500, months = 4)
#> [1] 14000
emergency_fund_target(monthly_expenses = 3500, months = 6)
#> [1] 21000


Build the essential expenses number from its parts first. These categories match the book’s baseline table.


show/hide
essentials <- c(housing = 1600, groceries = 550, utilities = 300,
                transportation = 600, health = 250, min_debt = 200)
sum(essentials)
#> [1] 3500


Different households land in different places on the risk chart. outer() shows every combination of expense level and months.


show/hide
expenses <- c(2500, 3500, 5000)
months   <- c(3, 4, 6, 9)
grid <- outer(expenses, months, emergency_fund_target)
dimnames(grid) <- list(paste0("$", expenses, "/mo"), paste(months, "mo"))
grid
#>           3 mo  4 mo  6 mo  9 mo
#> $2500/mo  7500 10000 15000 22500
#> $3500/mo 10500 14000 21000 31500
#> $5000/mo 15000 20000 30000 45000


Sanity check: the $1,000 starter fund covers well under one month of essentials, which is why it is a first step and not the finish line.


show/hide
1000 / 3500
#> [1] 0.2857143


How to read this: pick your row by essential expenses and your column by risk. A stable, single household spending $3,500 might choose 4 months ($14,000); a self-employed one might choose 9 ($31,500).


The Python version of emergency_fund_target() works the same way.


show/hide
def emergency_fund_target(monthly_expenses, months=3):
    return monthly_expenses * months

print(emergency_fund_target(monthly_expenses=3500, months=3))
#> 10500
print(emergency_fund_target(monthly_expenses=3500, months=4))
#> 14000
print(emergency_fund_target(monthly_expenses=3500, months=6))
#> 21000


Build the essential expenses number from its parts first.


show/hide
essentials = {"housing": 1600, "groceries": 550, "utilities": 300,
              "transportation": 600, "health": 250, "min_debt": 200}
sum(essentials.values())
#> 3500


Every combination of expense level and months.


show/hide
expenses = [2500, 3500, 5000]
months = [3, 4, 6, 9]
print("           " + "".join(f"{m:>9} mo" for m in months))
#>                    3 mo        4 mo        6 mo        9 mo
for e in expenses:
    row = "".join(f"{emergency_fund_target(e, m):>12,}" for m in months)
    print(f"${e:,}/mo  {row}")
#> $2,500/mo         7,500      10,000      15,000      22,500
#> $3,500/mo        10,500      14,000      21,000      31,500
#> $5,000/mo        15,000      20,000      30,000      45,000


Sanity check: the $1,000 starter fund covers well under one month of essentials.


show/hide
round(1000 / 3500, 2)
#> 0.29


How to read this: pick your row by essential expenses and your column by risk. A stable, single household spending $3,500 might choose 4 months ($14,000); a self-employed one might choose 9 ($31,500).


Assuming essential monthly expenses are in cell A2 and the number of months is in B2:
=A2*B2
To build the baseline, list essential categories in D2:D7 with amounts in E2:E7, and put =SUM(E2:E7) in A2.
For a grid, put expense levels down A5:A7 and months across B4:E4. In B5, enter the formula below and fill right and down:
=$A5*B$4

title: Emergency Fund
text:
3 Months to Reach Your Target
Given your current balance and a monthly contribution, how long until you reach the target? Part of the target bar is already filled; the monthly contributions close the gap.
Formula: Months to Goal = (Target − Current Balance) ÷ Monthly Contribution
Book example: a $14,000 target with $2,000 saved and $500/month takes (14,000 − 2,000) ÷ 500 = 24 months.





A $14,000 target with $2,000 saved: the $12,000 gap, filled $500 at a time







A $14,000 target with $2,000 saved: the $12,000 gap, filled $500 at a time





RPythonExcel


months_to_ef_goal() subtracts what you have saved from the target, divides by the contribution, and rounds up to whole months.


show/hide
months_to_ef_goal <- function(target, current_balance, monthly_contribution) {
  remaining <- max(0, target - current_balance)
  ceiling(remaining / monthly_contribution)
}

months_to_ef_goal(target = 14000, current_balance = 2000, monthly_contribution = 500)
#> [1] 24


Compare the three contribution levels from the book’s building chart. max() is not vectorized over targets, but the contribution argument is, so this works directly.


show/hide
contributions <- c(300, 500, 750, 1000)
data.frame(
  contribution = contributions,
  months       = months_to_ef_goal(14000, 2000, contributions)
)
#> # A tibble: 4 × 2
#>   contribution months
#>          <dbl>  <dbl>
#> 1          300     40
#> 2          500     24
#> 3          750     16
#> 4         1000     12


Edge cases: a fund that is already full needs 0 months, and a gap that does not divide evenly needs one extra, smaller final month.


show/hide
months_to_ef_goal(14000, current_balance = 15000, monthly_contribution = 500)
#> [1] 0
months_to_ef_goal(14000, current_balance = 1900, monthly_contribution = 500)
#> [1] 25


How to read this: going from $500 to $1,000 a month cuts 24 months to 12. Doubling the contribution halves the wait.


The Python version of months_to_ef_goal() works the same way.


show/hide
import math

def months_to_ef_goal(target, current_balance, monthly_contribution):
    remaining = max(0, target - current_balance)
    return math.ceil(remaining / monthly_contribution)

print(months_to_ef_goal(target=14000, current_balance=2000, monthly_contribution=500))
#> 24


Compare several contribution levels.


show/hide
for c in [300, 500, 750, 1000]:
    print(f"${c:>5,}/month -> {months_to_ef_goal(14000, 2000, c):>3} months")
#> $  300/month ->  40 months
#> $  500/month ->  24 months
#> $  750/month ->  16 months
#> $1,000/month ->  12 months


Edge cases: a full fund needs 0 months, and an uneven gap needs one extra, smaller final month.


show/hide
print(months_to_ef_goal(14000, 15000, 500))
#> 0
print(months_to_ef_goal(14000, 1900, 500))
#> 25


How to read this: going from $500 to $1,000 a month cuts 24 months to 12. Doubling the contribution halves the wait.


Assuming the target is in A2, your current balance is in B2, and your monthly contribution is in C2:
=ROUNDUP(MAX(0, A2-B2)/C2, 0)
To compare contributions, keep the target in A2 and balance in B2, list contributions down C2:C5, and in D2 enter the formula below and fill down:
=ROUNDUP(MAX(0, $A$2-$B$2)/C2, 0)

title: Emergency Fund
text:
4 Contribution Needed by a Deadline
Working backwards: to reach the target by a set month, how much do you need to save each month? The number of slices is fixed, and the question is how wide each slice must be.
Formula: Monthly Contribution = (Target − Current Balance) ÷ Months Remaining
Book example: a $14,000 fund in 18 months with $2,000 saved needs (14,000 − 2,000) ÷ 18 = $667/month.





The same $12,000 gap, cut into 18 equal monthly slices







The same $12,000 gap, cut into 18 equal monthly slices





RPythonExcel


monthly_contribution_needed() flips the question: given a deadline, it returns the monthly amount, rounded up to the next dollar.


show/hide
monthly_contribution_needed <- function(target, current_balance, months) {
  remaining <- max(0, target - current_balance)
  ceiling(remaining / months)
}

monthly_contribution_needed(target = 14000, current_balance = 2000, months = 18)
#> [1] 667


Compare a few deadlines.


show/hide
deadlines <- c(12, 18, 24, 36)
data.frame(
  months  = deadlines,
  monthly = monthly_contribution_needed(14000, 2000, deadlines)
)
#> # A tibble: 4 × 2
#>   months monthly
#>    <dbl>   <dbl>
#> 1     12    1000
#> 2     18     667
#> 3     24     500
#> 4     36     334


Sanity check: rounding up means 18 payments of $667 slightly overshoot the $12,000 gap, so you finish on time.


show/hide
667 * 18
#> [1] 12006
ceiling(12000 / 667)
#> [1] 18


How to read this: if $667 does not fit your budget, stretch the deadline. Moving from 18 to 24 months drops the payment to $500.


The Python version of monthly_contribution_needed() works the same way.


show/hide
import math

def monthly_contribution_needed(target, current_balance, months):
    remaining = max(0, target - current_balance)
    return math.ceil(remaining / months)

print(monthly_contribution_needed(target=14000, current_balance=2000, months=18))
#> 667


Compare a few deadlines.


show/hide
for m in [12, 18, 24, 36]:
    print(f"{m:>2} months -> ${monthly_contribution_needed(14000, 2000, m):,}/month")
#> 12 months -> $1,000/month
#> 18 months -> $667/month
#> 24 months -> $500/month
#> 36 months -> $334/month


Sanity check: 18 payments of $667 slightly overshoot the $12,000 gap.


show/hide
print(667 * 18, math.ceil(12000 / 667))
#> 12006 18


How to read this: if $667 does not fit your budget, stretch the deadline. Moving from 18 to 24 months drops the payment to $500.


Assuming the target is in A2, your current balance is in B2, and the number of months is in C2:
=ROUNDUP(MAX(0, A2-B2)/C2, 0)
To compare deadlines, list months down C2:C5 and in D2 enter the formula below and fill down:
=ROUNDUP(MAX(0, $A$2-$B$2)/C2, 0)

title: Emergency Fund
section: 5 What the Fund Earns While You Build It
text:
5 What the Fund Earns While You Build It
A fund in a high-yield savings account earns interest. It will not change your timeline much, but it is real money. Each month the balance is multiplied by (1 + the monthly rate).
Formula: Future Value = Balance × (1 + monthly rate)^months, where monthly rate = annual rate ÷ 12
Book example: $14,000 at 4.5%, untouched for 12 months, grows to about $14,643.





$14,000 at 4.5% for 12 months: your balance plus interest







$14,000 at 4.5% for 12 months: your balance plus interest





RPythonExcel


ef_growth() grows a balance month by month at a given annual rate.


show/hide
ef_growth <- function(balance, annual_rate, months) {
  monthly_rate <- annual_rate / 12
  balance * (1 + monthly_rate)^months
}

ef_growth(balance = 14000, annual_rate = 0.045, months = 12)
#> [1] 14643.16


Where you park the fund matters. Compare a typical big bank savings rate with a high-yield account.


show/hide
rates <- c(big_bank = 0.0001, hysa_low = 0.035, hysa = 0.045)
interest <- ef_growth(14000, rates, 12) - 14000
round(interest, 2)
#> big_bank hysa_low     hysa 
#>     1.40   497.94   643.16


Interest builds a little faster each month. Here is the running total at each quarter.


show/hide
qtrs <- c(3, 6, 9, 12)
data.frame(month = qtrs, interest = round(ef_growth(14000, 0.045, qtrs) - 14000, 2))
#> # A tibble: 4 × 2
#>   month interest
#>   <dbl>    <dbl>
#> 1     3     158.
#> 2     6     318.
#> 3     9     480.
#> 4    12     643.


Sanity check: banks usually quote APY, which already includes compounding. If 4.5% is the APY, the year-end balance is simply $14,000 × 1.045 = $14,630. The formula above treats 4.5% as a rate compounded monthly, which gives about $13 more.


show/hide
14000 * 1.045
#> [1] 14630


How to read this: roughly $630 to $645 a year is enough to cover a small car repair without touching the fund. At a big bank rate, the same money earns about $1.


The Python version of ef_growth() works the same way.


show/hide
def ef_growth(balance, annual_rate, months):
    monthly_rate = annual_rate / 12
    return balance * (1 + monthly_rate) ** months

print(ef_growth(balance=14000, annual_rate=0.045, months=12))
#> 14643.157550568254


Compare where you park the fund.


show/hide
rates = {"big_bank": 0.0001, "hysa_low": 0.035, "hysa": 0.045}
for name, r in rates.items():
    print(f"{name:<9} ${ef_growth(14000, r, 12) - 14000:>7,.2f} interest")
#> big_bank  $   1.40 interest
#> hysa_low  $ 497.94 interest
#> hysa      $ 643.16 interest


The running total of interest at each quarter.


show/hide
for m in [3, 6, 9, 12]:
    print(f"month {m:>2}: ${ef_growth(14000, 0.045, m) - 14000:,.2f}")
#> month  3: $158.09
#> month  6: $317.97
#> month  9: $479.65
#> month 12: $643.16


Sanity check: if 4.5% is the APY, the year-end balance is simply $14,000 × 1.045. Treating 4.5% as a monthly compounded rate gives about $13 more.


show/hide
print(round(14000 * 1.045, 2))
#> 14630.0


How to read this: roughly $630 to $645 a year is enough to cover a small car repair without touching the fund. At a big bank rate, the same money earns about $1.


Assuming the balance is in A2, the annual rate is in B2 (as a decimal), and the number of months is in C2:
=A2*(1+B2/12)^C2
Interest earned on its own is the future value minus the balance:
=A2*(1+B2/12)^C2 - A2
If the bank quotes an APY in B2 and you hold for a full year, this gives the exact year-end balance:
=A2*(1+B2)

title: Financial Goals
section: 2 Saving for a Goal with Interest
text:
2 Saving for a Goal with Interest
Interest does part of the work, so you can save a little less each month than goal ÷ months. This formula works backward from the future value of a monthly deposit.
Formula: Monthly amount = Goal × r ÷ ((1 + r)^n − 1), where r = yearly rate ÷ 12 and n = number of months





A $15,000 goal in 5 years at 4%: your deposits plus interest







A $15,000 goal in 5 years at 4%: your deposits plus interest




Example: a $15,000 down payment in 5 years at 4% takes about $226 a month, $24 less than the $250 you’d need with no interest. Over five years, interest adds about $1,425.

RPythonExcel


monthly_for_goal() returns the monthly deposit. A rate of zero falls back to plain division.


show/hide
monthly_for_goal <- function(goal, annual_rate, months) {
  r <- annual_rate / 12
  if (r == 0) return(goal / months)
  goal * r / ((1 + r)^months - 1)
}

# $15,000 in 5 years at 4%, compared to no interest
monthly_for_goal(goal = 15000, annual_rate = 0.04, months = 60)
#> [1] 226.2478
monthly_for_goal(goal = 15000, annual_rate = 0, months = 60)
#> [1] 250


How much of the goal comes from interest? Multiply the deposit by the number of months and subtract from the goal.


show/hide
pmt <- monthly_for_goal(goal = 15000, annual_rate = 0.04, months = 60)
c(deposits = pmt * 60, interest = 15000 - pmt * 60)
#> deposits interest 
#> 13574.87  1425.13


Same goal, different rates and deadlines. A longer runway lowers the monthly amount far more than a higher rate does.


show/hide
grid <- expand.grid(annual_rate = c(0, 0.02, 0.04, 0.05), years = c(3, 5, 7))
grid$monthly <- round(mapply(monthly_for_goal, goal = 15000,
                             annual_rate = grid$annual_rate,
                             months = grid$years * 12))
grid
#> # A tibble: 12 × 3
#>    annual_rate years monthly
#>          <dbl> <dbl>   <dbl>
#>  1        0        3     417
#>  2        0.02     3     405
#>  3        0.04     3     393
#>  4        0.05     3     387
#>  5        0        5     250
#>  6        0.02     5     238
#>  7        0.04     5     226
#>  8        0.05     5     221
#>  9        0        7     179
#> 10        0.02     7     167
#> 11        0.04     7     155
#> 12        0.05     7     150


Sanity check: growing $226.25 a month at 4% for 60 months should land back on $15,000.


show/hide
r <- 0.04 / 12
pmt * ((1 + r)^60 - 1) / r
#> [1] 15000




monthly_for_goal() returns the monthly deposit. A rate of zero falls back to plain division.


show/hide
def monthly_for_goal(goal, annual_rate, months):
    r = annual_rate / 12
    if r == 0:
        return goal / months
    return goal * r / ((1 + r) ** months - 1)

# $15,000 in 5 years at 4%, compared to no interest
print(monthly_for_goal(goal=15000, annual_rate=0.04, months=60))
#> 226.24783082898958
print(monthly_for_goal(goal=15000, annual_rate=0, months=60))
#> 250.0


How much of the goal comes from interest?


show/hide
pmt = monthly_for_goal(goal=15000, annual_rate=0.04, months=60)
print(f"deposits: {pmt * 60:,.2f}  interest: {15000 - pmt * 60:,.2f}")
#> deposits: 13,574.87  interest: 1,425.13


Same goal, different rates and deadlines:


show/hide
print(f"{'rate':>6} {'3 yrs':>7} {'5 yrs':>7} {'7 yrs':>7}")
#>   rate   3 yrs   5 yrs   7 yrs
for rate in [0, 0.02, 0.04, 0.05]:
    row = [monthly_for_goal(15000, rate, y * 12) for y in [3, 5, 7]]
    print(f"{rate:>6.0%} " + " ".join(f"{m:>7,.0f}" for m in row))
#>     0%     417     250     179
#>     2%     405     238     167
#>     4%     393     226     155
#>     5%     387     221     150


Sanity check: the deposits should grow back to $15,000.


show/hide
r = 0.04 / 12
print(round(pmt * ((1 + r) ** 60 - 1) / r, 2))
#> 15000.0




Assuming the goal is in B2, the yearly rate is in C2, and the number of months is in D2, the monthly amount goes in E2:
=PMT(C2 / 12, D2, 0, -B2)
Interest earned goes in F2:
=B2 - E2 * D2
To check the answer, FV() should return the goal:
=FV(C2 / 12, D2, -E2)



How to read this result: the monthly amount is your payday transfer. If it doesn’t fit your budget, push the date out before you lower the goal; an extra two years cuts the monthly amount by about 30%.

title: Financial Goals
section: 3 One Goal at a Time vs. All at Once
text:
3 One Goal at a Time vs. All at Once
When several goals share one monthly savings amount, the order changes when the first goal finishes. It never changes when the last one finishes.
Formula: Months to finish all goals = Total of all goals ÷ Monthly savings; Months to finish the first goal = First goal ÷ Amount going to it each month





Two goals funded with $600/month: one at a time vs. split evenly







Two goals funded with $600/month: one at a time vs. split evenly




Example: with $600 a month for a $3,000 trip and a $9,000 car, both goals are done in ($3,000 + $9,000) ÷ $600 = 20 months either way. The trip takes 5 months one at a time, or 10 months split evenly.

RPythonExcel


months_to_fund() rounds up, since a goal isn’t done until the last dollar is in.


show/hide
months_to_fund <- function(goal, monthly) {
  ceiling(goal / monthly)
}

# one at a time: trip first, then car
months_to_fund(3000, 600)
#> [1] 5
months_to_fund(3000 + 9000, 600)
#> [1] 20

# split evenly: trip gets half until it's done
months_to_fund(3000, 300)
#> [1] 10
months_to_fund(3000 + 9000, 600)
#> [1] 20


Try other splits. The more you send to the trip, the sooner it’s done. The car always finishes at month 20, as long as every dollar keeps going to some goal.


show/hide
trip_share <- c(1, 0.75, 0.5, 0.25)
data.frame(
  trip_share  = trip_share,
  trip_month  = months_to_fund(3000, 600 * trip_share),
  all_done    = months_to_fund(3000 + 9000, 600)
)
#> # A tibble: 4 × 3
#>   trip_share trip_month all_done
#>        <dbl>      <dbl>    <dbl>
#> 1       1             5       20
#> 2       0.75          7       20
#> 3       0.5          10       20
#> 4       0.25         20       20


Edge case: rounding up matters. A $1,000 goal at $300 a month takes 4 months, not 3.3.


show/hide
months_to_fund(1000, 300)
#> [1] 4




months_to_fund() rounds up, since a goal isn’t done until the last dollar is in.


show/hide
import math

def months_to_fund(goal, monthly):
    return math.ceil(goal / monthly)

# one at a time: trip first, then car
print(months_to_fund(3000, 600), months_to_fund(3000 + 9000, 600))
#> 5 20

# split evenly: trip gets half until it's done
print(months_to_fund(3000, 300), months_to_fund(3000 + 9000, 600))
#> 10 20


Try other splits:


show/hide
print(f"{'trip share':>10} {'trip month':>10} {'all done':>9}")
#> trip share trip month  all done
for share in [1, 0.75, 0.5, 0.25]:
    print(f"{share:>10.0%} {months_to_fund(3000, 600 * share):>10} "
          f"{months_to_fund(3000 + 9000, 600):>9}")
#>       100%          5        20
#>        75%          7        20
#>        50%         10        20
#>        25%         20        20


Edge case: rounding up matters.


show/hide
print(months_to_fund(1000, 300))
#> 4




Assuming the goal is in B2 and the monthly amount going to it is in C2:
=ROUNDUP(B2 / C2, 0)
For the finish line on all goals, put the goals in B2:B3 and total monthly savings in D2:
=ROUNDUP(SUM(B2:B3) / D2, 0)



How to read this result: the order is a choice about which goal you want first, not about saving time overall. Put a fixed date goal (a wedding, a car on its last legs) first, or give it the bigger share.

title: Asset Allocation
text:
Stocks, bonds, and cash: stocks grow most but can drop 30% to 50%; bonds grow slower and fall less; cash is the emergency fund and sits outside the investment split
How much in stocks when you’re young: everyone agrees on mostly stocks; Bogle (roughly your age in bonds, later 80 to 85% stocks), Sethi (80 to 90%), Collins (100% while building), Felix on the Cederburg research (100% stocks, global), Housel (extra cash for peace of mind); 80 to 90% is a reasonable start
US vs. international: 60/40 to 80/20 (US/international) is common; the Cederburg research goes to about one third US
Target date funds: one fund that sets the split and follows a glide path toward bonds; check the fee and don’t mix it with other funds
The three fund portfolio: total US stocks, total international stocks, total US bonds for about 0.05% (for example 60/30/10)
Rebalancing: check once a year and act when any part drifts more than about 5 percentage points; send new money to whatever is below target

title: Asset Allocation
text:
2 Good Years and Bad Years
A portfolio’s return is a weighted average of what each part earns.
Formula: Portfolio return = (Stock % × Stock return) + (Bond % × Bond return)
Example (stocks +10% average, −40% bad; bonds +4% average, 0% bad): an 80/20 split in a bad year is (0.80 × −40%) + (0.20 × 0%) = −32%, or −$3,200 on $10,000. In an average year it’s (0.80 × 10%) + (0.20 × 4%) = 8.8%, or +$880.





$10,000 in an average year and a bad year, by stock/bond split







$10,000 in an average year and a bad year, by stock/bond split




The second example adds more splits and two columns compared with 100/0: the average year gain you give up and the bad year loss you avoid. The third uses the real 2008 numbers from the book (stocks about −37%, bonds about +5%), where bonds actually went up.

RPythonExcel




show/hide
portfolio_return <- function(stock_pct, stock_return, bond_return) {
  stock_pct * stock_return + (1 - stock_pct) * bond_return
}

# 100/0, 80/20, and 60/40 in an average year and a bad year
splits <- c(1, 0.8, 0.6)
data.frame(
  stocks  = splits,
  average = portfolio_return(splits, stock_return = 0.10, bond_return = 0.04),
  bad     = portfolio_return(splits, stock_return = -0.40, bond_return = 0)
)

title: Asset Allocation
section: 3 How Much to Move When You Rebalance
text:
3 How Much to Move When You Rebalance
When one part grows or shrinks, move just enough to get back to the target split.
Formula: Amount to move = (Target % × Total) − Current amount
Example: $10,000 at 80/20, then stocks drop 30%. Stocks are $5,600, bonds $2,000, total $7,600 (stocks about 74%). (0.80 × $7,600) − $5,600 = $480 moved from bonds into stocks.





An 80/20 portfolio before a 30% stock drop, after it, and after rebalancing







An 80/20 portfolio before a 30% stock drop, after it, and after rebalancing




The second example runs several stock moves, up and down, and applies the book’s 5 percentage point rule to decide whether to act at all. A negative amount means sell stocks and buy bonds. The last example rebalances with new money only, so nothing gets sold.

RPythonExcel




show/hide
rebalance_amount <- function(target_pct, total, current_amount) {
  target_pct * total - current_amount
}

# $5,600 in stocks and $2,000 in bonds after a 30% stock drop
rebalance_amount(target_pct = 0.80, total = 5600 + 2000, current_amount = 5600)
#> [1] 480

# several stock moves on an 80/20, $10,000 portfolio
move   <- c(-0.30, -0.10, -0.05, 0.10, 0.30)
stocks <- 8000 * (1 + move)
bonds  <- 2000
total  <- stocks + bonds
data.frame(
  stock_move  = move * 100,
  stock_share = round(100 * stocks / total, 1),
  drift_pts   = round(100 * stocks / total - 80, 1),
  rebalance   = abs(100 * stocks / total - 80) > 5,
  move_amount = round(rebalance_amount(0.80, total, stocks))
)
#> # A tibble: 5 × 5
#>   stock_move stock_share drift_pts rebalance
#>        <dbl>       <dbl>     <dbl> <lgl>    
#> 1        -30        73.7      -6.3 TRUE     
#> 2        -10        78.3      -1.7 FALSE    
#> 3         -5        79.2      -0.8 FALSE    
#> 4         10        81.5       1.5 FALSE    
#> 5         30        83.9       3.9 FALSE    
#> # ℹ 1 more variable: move_amount <dbl>

# rebalance with new money: how much of a new deposit goes to stocks?
# (only works if the deposit is big enough; otherwise put it all in stocks)
new_money <- 1000
min(new_money, rebalance_amount(0.80, 7600 + new_money, 5600))
#> [1] 1000






show/hide
def rebalance_amount(target_pct, total, current_amount):
    return target_pct * total - current_amount

# $5,600 in stocks and $2,000 in bonds after a 30% stock drop
print(rebalance_amount(target_pct=0.80, total=5600 + 2000, current_amount=5600))
#> 480.0

# several stock moves on an 80/20, $10,000 portfolio
for move in [-0.30, -0.10, -0.05, 0.10, 0.30]:
    stocks = 8000 * (1 + move)
    total = stocks + 2000
    drift = 100 * stocks / total - 80
    amt = rebalance_amount(0.80, total, stocks)
    print(f"stocks {move:+.0%}: share {stocks / total:.1%}, drift {drift:+.1f} pts, "
          f"rebalance {abs(drift) > 5}, move ${amt:,.0f}")
#> stocks -30%: share 73.7%, drift -6.3 pts, rebalance True, move $480
#> stocks -10%: share 78.3%, drift -1.7 pts, rebalance False, move $160
#> stocks -5%: share 79.2%, drift -0.8 pts, rebalance False, move $80
#> stocks +10%: share 81.5%, drift +1.5 pts, rebalance False, move $-160
#> stocks +30%: share 83.9%, drift +3.9 pts, rebalance False, move $-480

# rebalance with new money
new_money = 1000
print(min(new_money, rebalance_amount(0.80, 7600 + new_money, 5600)))
#> 1000




With Target % in B2, Stocks in C2, and Bonds in D2:
=B2 * (C2 + D2) - C2
To flag whether the drift is more than 5 points:
=ABS(C2/(C2+D2) - B2) > 0.05



Read a positive answer as “buy that much stock,” and a negative answer as “sell that much stock.” A 10% drop only moves the split about 2 points, so the 5 point rule says wait. With $1,000 of new money after the 30% drop, the full $1,000 goes to stocks and the gap closes from $480 to under $300 without selling anything.

title: Budgeting
text:
Mindset shift: a budget is intentional allocation, not restriction; reframe “I have to spend” as “my needs cost”; room for error is the most underrated concept (Housel)

title: Budgeting
text:
2 Percentages
The foundational budgeting calculation: what share of income does each expense represent? Picture income as one bar and each expense as a slice of it.
Formula: (Expense ÷ Income) × 100
Book example: rent of $1,500 on $5,000 of take-home pay is 30% of income.





Rent ($1,500) as a share of a $5,000 paycheck







Rent ($1,500) as a share of a $5,000 paycheck





RPythonExcel


percent_of_income() divides an expense by income and multiplies by 100.


show/hide
percent_of_income <- function(expense, income) {
  (expense / income) * 100
}

percent_of_income(expense = 1500, income = 5000)
#> [1] 30


The function is vectorized, so we can pass the whole zero-based budget from the book at once.


show/hide
zero_based <- data.frame(
  category = c("Rent", "Groceries", "Transport", "Investments",
               "Savings", "Fun Money", "Other"),
  amount   = c(1500, 500, 300, 1000, 500, 700, 500)
)
zero_based$pct <- percent_of_income(zero_based$amount, income = 5000)
zero_based
#> # A tibble: 7 × 3
#>   category    amount   pct
#>   <chr>        <dbl> <dbl>
#> 1 Rent          1500    30
#> 2 Groceries      500    10
#> 3 Transport      300     6
#> 4 Investments   1000    20
#> 5 Savings        500    10
#> 6 Fun Money      700    14
#> 7 Other          500    10


Sanity check: in a zero-based budget, the dollars add up to income and the percentages add up to 100.


show/hide
sum(zero_based$amount)
#> [1] 5000
sum(zero_based$pct)
#> [1] 100


How to read this: rent is 30% of take-home pay, and every category together uses 100%. If the total were above 100, the budget would spend more than you earn.
One edge case: an income of zero has no meaningful percentage. R returns Inf (or NaN for 0 ÷ 0) instead of an error.


show/hide
percent_of_income(expense = 1500, income = 0)
#> [1] Inf




The Python version of percent_of_income() works the same way.


show/hide
def percent_of_income(expense, income):
    return (expense / income) * 100

percent_of_income(expense=1500, income=5000)
#> 30.0


Plain Python works one value at a time, so we loop over the zero-based budget from the book.


show/hide
zero_based = {
    "Rent": 1500, "Groceries": 500, "Transport": 300, "Investments": 1000,
    "Savings": 500, "Fun Money": 700, "Other": 500,
}
for category, amount in zero_based.items():
    print(f"{category:<12} ${amount:>6,}  {percent_of_income(amount, 5000):5.1f}%")
#> Rent         $ 1,500   30.0%
#> Groceries    $   500   10.0%
#> Transport    $   300    6.0%
#> Investments  $ 1,000   20.0%
#> Savings      $   500   10.0%
#> Fun Money    $   700   14.0%
#> Other        $   500   10.0%


Sanity check: the dollars add up to income and the percentages add up to 100.


show/hide
total = sum(zero_based.values())
print(total, percent_of_income(total, 5000))
#> 5000 100.0


How to read this: rent is 30% of take-home pay, and every category together uses 100%. If the total were above 100, the budget would spend more than you earn.
One edge case: Python raises a ZeroDivisionError when income is zero, so guard against it.


show/hide
def safe_percent_of_income(expense, income):
    if income == 0:
        return None
    return percent_of_income(expense, income)

print(safe_percent_of_income(1500, 0))
#> None




Assuming Expense is in cell B2 and Income is in cell C2:
=(B2 / C2) * 100





Or, more simply, enter =B2 / C2 and format the cell as a Percentage using the button in the toolbar.





For the full zero-based budget, put category names in A2:A8, amounts in B2:B8, and income in E1. In C2, lock the income cell with $ and fill down to C8:
=B2 / $E$1
Check the totals in row 9. B9 should equal income, and C9 should read 100%:
=SUM(B2:B8)
=SUM(C2:C8)

title: Budgeting
text:
3 Annualizing and Monthly-izing
Scale any spending habit across time periods to see the true cost. Each period is the shorter one multiplied by how many times it fits.
Formula: Cost over a longer period = Cost per period × Number of periods it contains
Daily → Weekly: × 7
Weekly → Monthly: × 4.33 (not 4)
Monthly → Annual: × 12
Daily → Annual: × 365
Annual → Monthly: ÷ 12
Book example: a $5 daily coffee is $5 × 365 = $1,825 per year.





The same $5/day habit across four time periods







The same $5/day habit across four time periods





RPythonExcel


to_annual() multiplies a recurring amount by how many times it happens in a year. to_monthly() converts any period to a monthly amount.


show/hide
to_annual <- function(amount, period = c("daily", "weekly", "monthly")) {
  period  <- match.arg(period)
  factors <- c(daily = 365, weekly = 52, monthly = 12)
  amount * factors[[period]]
}

to_monthly <- function(amount, period = c("daily", "weekly", "annual")) {
  period  <- match.arg(period)
  factors <- c(daily = 30.44, weekly = 4.33, annual = 1 / 12)
  amount * factors[[period]]
}


The book examples: a $5/day coffee over a year, and $150/week on groceries over a month.


show/hide
to_annual(amount = 5, period = "daily")
#> [1] 1825
to_monthly(amount = 150, period = "weekly")
#> [1] 649.5


Several habits side by side. mapply() runs both functions over each row.


show/hide
habits <- data.frame(
  habit  = c("Coffee", "Groceries", "Streaming"),
  amount = c(5, 150, 15.99),
  period = c("daily", "weekly", "monthly")
)
habits$annual  <- mapply(to_annual, habits$amount, habits$period)
habits$monthly <- habits$annual / 12
habits
#> # A tibble: 3 × 5
#>   habit     amount period  annual monthly
#>   <chr>      <dbl> <chr>    <dbl>   <dbl>
#> 1 Coffee       5   daily    1825    152. 
#> 2 Groceries  150   weekly   7800    650  
#> 3 Streaming   16.0 monthly   192.    16.0


The same math powers sinking funds. Divide each periodic cost from the book by 12 to get the monthly set aside.


show/hide
sinking <- data.frame(
  expense = c("Car insurance", "Christmas/gifts", "Car maintenance", "Annual vacation"),
  annual  = c(1200, 600, 1200, 2400)
)
sinking$monthly <- to_monthly(sinking$annual, period = "annual")
sinking
#> # A tibble: 4 × 3
#>   expense         annual monthly
#>   <chr>            <dbl>   <dbl>
#> 1 Car insurance     1200     100
#> 2 Christmas/gifts    600      50
#> 3 Car maintenance   1200     100
#> 4 Annual vacation   2400     200
sum(sinking$monthly)
#> [1] 450


Sanity check: 4.33 weeks × 12 months is 51.96 weeks, a hair short of 52. That is why weekly → monthly → annual lands $6 under weekly → annual for $150/week.


show/hide
to_annual(150, "weekly")
#> [1] 7800
to_monthly(150, "weekly") * 12
#> [1] 7794


How to read this: the annual number is the one to compare against your goals. A $5 habit you never think about costs about as much as a vacation.


The Python versions use a dictionary of factors.


show/hide
def to_annual(amount, period="daily"):
    factors = {"daily": 365, "weekly": 52, "monthly": 12}
    return amount * factors[period]

def to_monthly(amount, period="daily"):
    factors = {"daily": 30.44, "weekly": 4.33, "annual": 1 / 12}
    return amount * factors[period]


The book examples: a $5/day coffee over a year, and $150/week on groceries over a month.


show/hide
print(to_annual(amount=5, period="daily"))
#> 1825
print(to_monthly(amount=150, period="weekly"))
#> 649.5


Several habits side by side.


show/hide
habits = [("Coffee", 5, "daily"), ("Groceries", 150, "weekly"), ("Streaming", 15.99, "monthly")]
for habit, amount, period in habits:
    annual = to_annual(amount, period)
    print(f"{habit:<10} annual ${annual:>9,.2f}  monthly ${annual / 12:>7,.2f}")
#> Coffee     annual $ 1,825.00  monthly $ 152.08
#> Groceries  annual $ 7,800.00  monthly $ 650.00
#> Streaming  annual $   191.88  monthly $  15.99


The same math powers sinking funds. Divide each periodic cost from the book by 12.


show/hide
sinking = {"Car insurance": 1200, "Christmas/gifts": 600,
           "Car maintenance": 1200, "Annual vacation": 2400}
monthly = {k: to_monthly(v, period="annual") for k, v in sinking.items()}
for k, v in monthly.items():
    print(f"{k:<16} ${v:,.2f}/month")
#> Car insurance    $100.00/month
#> Christmas/gifts  $50.00/month
#> Car maintenance  $100.00/month
#> Annual vacation  $200.00/month
print(f"Total: ${sum(monthly.values()):,.2f}/month")
#> Total: $450.00/month


Sanity check: 4.33 × 12 = 51.96 weeks, so the two routes differ by about $6 on $150/week.


show/hide
print(to_annual(150, "weekly"), round(to_monthly(150, "weekly") * 12, 2))
#> 7800 7794.0


How to read this: the annual number is the one to compare against your goals. A $5 habit you never think about costs about as much as a vacation.


Let’s start with the daily value in cell A1, then convert it to the cost per week in cell A2:
=A1 * 7
Next we can convert the week to the monthly cost in cell A3:
=A2 * 4.33
Finally, we get the annual cost in cell A4:
=A1 * 365
Format cells A1 - A4 as Currency or Accounting.





To convert a weekly value in cell A1 to a monthly value, place the following formula in cell A2:
=A1 * 4.33
To convert the monthly cost to an annual cost, enter the following in cell A3:
=A2 * 12
Format cells A1 - A3 as Currency or Accounting.





For a sinking fund tab, put expense names in A2:A5 and annual costs in B2:B5. In C2, enter the formula below and fill down, then total the column in C6 with =SUM(C2:C5):
=B2 / 12

title: Budgeting
text:
4 Opportunity Cost
Every dollar spent is also what that dollar could have become. The hidden cost of any purchase is its future value if invested instead.
Formula: amount × (1 + r)^n
Book example: choosing a $15,000 used car over a $40,000 new one and investing the $25,000 difference at 7% for 30 years gives $25,000 × (1.07)^30 ≈ $190,000.





$25,000 invested at 7%: value at each checkpoint







$25,000 invested at 7%: value at each checkpoint





RPythonExcel


opportunity_cost() takes the dollar amount, the yearly rate of return, and the number of years.


show/hide
opportunity_cost <- function(amount, rate, years) {
  amount * (1 + rate)^years
}

opportunity_cost(amount = 25000, rate = 0.07, years = 30)
#> [1] 190306.4


Returns are never guaranteed, so compare a cautious, middle, and hopeful rate across several horizons. outer() builds the whole grid in one call.


show/hide
years <- c(5, 10, 20, 30)
rates <- c(0.05, 0.07, 0.09)
grid <- outer(years, rates, function(y, r) opportunity_cost(25000, r, y))
dimnames(grid) <- list(paste(years, "yrs"), paste0(rates * 100, "%"))
round(grid)
#>            5%     7%     9%
#> 5 yrs   31907  35064  38466
#> 10 yrs  40722  49179  59184
#> 20 yrs  66332  96742 140110
#> 30 yrs 108049 190306 331692


Sanity check: at 0% the money just sits there, and after 0 years nothing has grown.


show/hide
opportunity_cost(25000, rate = 0, years = 30)
#> [1] 25000
opportunity_cost(25000, rate = 0.07, years = 0)
#> [1] 25000


How to read this: the 7% column is the book’s estimate, but even the 5% column shows the car choice is worth more than $100,000 after 30 years. The longer the horizon, the more the rate matters.


The Python version of opportunity_cost() works the same way.


show/hide
def opportunity_cost(amount, rate, years):
    return amount * (1 + rate) ** years

opportunity_cost(amount=25000, rate=0.07, years=30)
#> 190306.37606655105


A grid of horizons and rates. numpy broadcasting fills every combination at once.


show/hide
import numpy as np

years = np.array([5, 10, 20, 30])
rates = np.array([0.05, 0.07, 0.09])
grid = opportunity_cost(25000, rates[None, :], years[:, None])
print("         " + "".join(f"{r:>10.0%}" for r in rates))
#>                  5%        7%        9%
for y, row in zip(years, grid):
    print(f"{y:>2} yrs   " + "".join(f"{v:>10,.0f}" for v in row))
#>  5 yrs       31,907    35,064    38,466
#> 10 yrs       40,722    49,179    59,184
#> 20 yrs       66,332    96,742   140,110
#> 30 yrs      108,049   190,306   331,692


Sanity check: 0% growth or 0 years returns the original amount.


show/hide
print(opportunity_cost(25000, 0, 30), opportunity_cost(25000, 0.07, 0))
#> 25000 25000.0


How to read this: the 7% column is the book’s estimate, but even the 5% column shows the car choice is worth more than $100,000 after 30 years. The longer the horizon, the more the rate matters.


Assuming the initial amount is in cell A2, the annual rate (as a decimal, e.g., 0.07) is in B2, and the number of years is in C2:
=A2*(1+B2)^C2





For a grid, put the amount in A1, rates across B2:D2 (0.05, 0.07, 0.09), and years down A3:A6 (5, 10, 20, 30). In B3, enter the formula below and fill right and down. The $ signs keep the amount, the rate row, and the years column locked:
=$A$1*(1+B$2)^$A3

title: Budgeting
text:
5 Break-Even
Useful for evaluating memberships, subscriptions, refinances, or any purchase with an upfront cost and recurring savings. Break-even is the first month cumulative savings meets the upfront cost.
Formula: Upfront Cost ÷ Monthly Savings = months to break even
Book example: a $500 membership that saves $60/month breaks even in $500 ÷ $60 = 8.3 months.





$60/month savings accumulating toward a $500 upfront cost







$60/month savings accumulating toward a $500 upfront cost





RPythonExcel


months_to_break_even() divides the upfront cost by the monthly savings.


show/hide
months_to_break_even <- function(upfront_cost, monthly_savings) {
  upfront_cost / monthly_savings
}

months_to_break_even(upfront_cost = 500, monthly_savings = 60)
#> [1] 8.333333


Savings arrive in whole months, so round up to find the month you actually cross the line. That matches the first green bar in the chart.


show/hide
ceiling(months_to_break_even(500, 60))
#> [1] 9


Compare a few options at once.


show/hide
options_df <- data.frame(
  option  = c("Gym membership", "Warehouse club", "Refinance fee"),
  upfront = c(500, 65, 3000),
  savings = c(60, 15, 120)
)
options_df$months <- months_to_break_even(options_df$upfront, options_df$savings)
options_df$whole_months <- ceiling(options_df$months)
options_df
#> # A tibble: 3 × 5
#>   option       upfront savings months whole_months
#>   <chr>          <dbl>   <dbl>  <dbl>        <dbl>
#> 1 Gym members…     500      60   8.33            9
#> 2 Warehouse c…      65      15   4.33            5
#> 3 Refinance f…    3000     120  25              25


Edge case: if a purchase saves nothing (or costs more each month), it never breaks even. Check before dividing.


show/hide
months_to_break_even(500, 0)
#> [1] Inf
months_to_break_even(500, -10)
#> [1] -50


How to read this: the $500 membership pays for itself if you keep using it past month 9. If you are not sure you will last that long, skip it.


The Python version of months_to_break_even() works the same way.


show/hide
def months_to_break_even(upfront_cost, monthly_savings):
    return upfront_cost / monthly_savings

months_to_break_even(upfront_cost=500, monthly_savings=60)
#> 8.333333333333334


Round up to the month you actually cross the line.


show/hide
import math

math.ceil(months_to_break_even(500, 60))
#> 9


Compare a few options at once.


show/hide
options = [("Gym membership", 500, 60), ("Warehouse club", 65, 15), ("Refinance fee", 3000, 120)]
for option, upfront, savings in options:
    m = months_to_break_even(upfront, savings)
    print(f"{option:<15} {m:5.1f} months  (month {math.ceil(m)})")
#> Gym membership    8.3 months  (month 9)
#> Warehouse club    4.3 months  (month 5)
#> Refinance fee    25.0 months  (month 25)


Edge case: zero savings raises a ZeroDivisionError in Python, and negative savings gives a negative answer. Neither ever breaks even, so guard against both.


show/hide
def safe_break_even(upfront_cost, monthly_savings):
    if monthly_savings <= 0:
        return math.inf
    return months_to_break_even(upfront_cost, monthly_savings)

print(safe_break_even(500, 0), safe_break_even(500, -10))
#> inf inf


How to read this: the $500 membership pays for itself if you keep using it past month 9. If you are not sure you will last that long, skip it.


Assuming the upfront cost is in cell A2 and the monthly savings amount is in cell B2:
=A2 / B2





To round up to whole months and flag purchases that never break even, use this in C2 instead:
=IF(B2 <= 0, "Never", ROUNDUP(A2 / B2, 0))

title: Managing Debt
text:
Debt hierarchy: every debt has a price (its APR); toxic debt (15 to 29% APR: credit cards, payday loans) gets attacked first, moderate debt (5 to 10%: car loans, private student loans) gets paid down steadily, and strategic debt (3 to 7%: mortgages, federal student loans) gets paid on schedule
Credit cards: pay them off before nearly every other goal (except insurance deductibles and an employer match); the playbook is stop using them, negotiate the APR, pick avalanche or snowball, consider a 0% transfer or cheaper loan, and automate minimums; once paid in full monthly, use cards as a payment tool
Student loans: the return depends on the income premium the degree creates; the 1× rule caps total debt at your expected first year salary, which works out to roughly 14% of gross pay on a standard 10 year plan at 6.5%
Federal IDR plans: payments are a share of discretionary income (AGI minus a multiple of the poverty guideline); SAVE ended in March 2026, RAP starts July 2026 (1 to 10% of AGI, 30 years), IBR is the stable fallback, and PSLF forgives the rest after 10 years of public service
Pay off vs. invest: compare the loan rate to your expected after tax return (above 6% pay off, 4 to 6% do both, below 4% invest), then add a peace of mind premium
Car loans: depreciating assets financed at 7 to 9%; buy used, pay cash, keep loans under 36 months, follow the 20/4/10 rule
Debt and the FOO: high interest debt is step 3, low interest debt is step 9; moderate debt sits in between, after emergency reserves

title: Managing Debt
text:
2 APR vs. APY
Lenders quote the APR. You actually pay the APY, which is higher because interest compounds.
Formula: APY = (1 + APR ÷ n)^n − 1, where n is the number of compounding periods per year
Example: a 24% APR compounded daily is about 27.1% APY. On a $10,000 balance that is an extra $310 a year.





APR cost vs. APY cost on a $10,000 balance (24% APR, daily compounding)







APR cost vs. APY cost on a $10,000 balance (24% APR, daily compounding)




The gap grows as the APR grows. It also grows with how often interest compounds, but most of the jump happens going from yearly to monthly. Daily adds only a little more. If APR and APY are the same, interest compounds once a year.

RPythonExcel




show/hide
apr_to_apy <- function(apr, periods_per_year = 365) {
  (1 + apr / periods_per_year)^periods_per_year - 1
}

# 24% APR compounded daily
apr_to_apy(apr = 0.24)
#> [1] 0.2711489


Compare several card rates and compounding schedules, plus the hidden cost on a $10,000 balance:


show/hide
aprs <- c(0.15, 0.20, 0.24, 0.29)
data.frame(
  apr          = fmt_pct(aprs),
  yearly       = fmt_pct(apr_to_apy(aprs, 1), 2),
  monthly      = fmt_pct(apr_to_apy(aprs, 12), 2),
  daily        = fmt_pct(apr_to_apy(aprs, 365), 2),
  hidden_cost  = fmt_dollar(10000 * (apr_to_apy(aprs) - aprs), 0)
)
#> # A tibble: 4 × 5
#>   apr   yearly monthly daily  hidden_cost
#>   <chr> <chr>  <chr>   <chr>  <chr>      
#> 1 15%   15%    16.08%  16.18% $118       
#> 2 20%   20%    21.94%  22.13% $213       
#> 3 24%   24%    26.82%  27.11% $311       
#> 4 29%   29%    33.18%  33.63% $463






show/hide
def apr_to_apy(apr, periods_per_year=365):
    return (1 + apr / periods_per_year) ** periods_per_year - 1

# 24% APR compounded daily
apr_to_apy(apr=0.24)
#> 0.27114889144128895


Compare several card rates and compounding schedules, plus the hidden cost on a $10,000 balance:


show/hide
print(f"{'APR':>5} {'yearly':>8} {'monthly':>8} {'daily':>8} {'hidden':>8}")
#>   APR   yearly  monthly    daily   hidden
for apr in [0.15, 0.20, 0.24, 0.29]:
    hidden = 10000 * (apr_to_apy(apr) - apr)
    print(f"{apr:>5.0%} {apr_to_apy(apr, 1):>8.2%} {apr_to_apy(apr, 12):>8.2%} "
          f"{apr_to_apy(apr):>8.2%} {hidden:>8,.0f}")
#>   15%   15.00%   16.08%   16.18%      118
#>   20%   20.00%   21.94%   22.13%      213
#>   24%   24.00%   26.82%   27.11%      311
#>   29%   29.00%   33.18%   33.63%      463




With the APR in A2 (as a decimal) and the compounding periods per year in B2:
=(1+A2/B2)^B2-1
The built in EFFECT() function gives the same number:
=EFFECT(A2, B2)
For the hidden cost on a balance in C2, put this in D2:
=C2*(EFFECT(A2, B2)-A2)

title: Managing Debt
text:
3 Minimum Payments
Minimum payments barely touch the balance. Most of each payment goes to interest. As the balance falls, a little more of each payment goes to principal, and the formula accounts for that.
Formula: Months to pay off = −ln(1 − r × Balance ÷ Payment) ÷ ln(1 + r), where r = APR ÷ 12
Example: $5,000 at 22% APR, paying $100 a month. The first month’s interest is about $92, so only $8 reduces the balance. Payoff takes about 137 months (11 years), and you pay about $13,700 in total.





Where a $100 minimum payment actually goes







Where a $100 minimum payment actually goes




The formula only works when the payment is bigger than the first month’s interest. If it isn’t, the balance never shrinks, and the answer comes back as NaN (not a number). Small increases in the payment cut years off the debt.

RPythonExcel




show/hide
months_to_payoff <- function(balance, monthly_payment, apr) {
  r <- apr / 12
  -log(1 - r * balance / monthly_payment) / log(1 + r)
}

# $5,000 balance, $100/month, 22% APR
months_to_payoff(balance = 5000, monthly_payment = 100, apr = 0.22)
#> [1] 136.7791


What happens if you pay more each month? Total paid is roughly months × payment (the last payment is usually a bit smaller).


show/hide
payments <- c(100, 150, 200, 300)
months   <- months_to_payoff(balance = 5000, monthly_payment = payments, apr = 0.22)
data.frame(
  payment        = fmt_dollar(payments, 0),
  months         = round(months),
  years          = round(months / 12, 1),
  total_paid     = fmt_dollar(months * payments, 0),
  total_interest = fmt_dollar(months * payments - 5000, 0)
)
#> # A tibble: 4 × 5
#>   payment months years total_paid total_interest
#>   <chr>    <dbl> <dbl> <chr>      <chr>         
#> 1 $100       137  11.4 $13,678    $8,678        
#> 2 $150        52   4.3 $7,798     $2,798        
#> 3 $200        34   2.8 $6,750     $1,750        
#> 4 $300        20   1.7 $6,021     $1,021


Sanity check: the payment must beat the first month’s interest.


show/hide
first_interest <- 5000 * 0.22 / 12
first_interest
#> [1] 91.66667
100 > first_interest
#> [1] TRUE
90 > first_interest
#> [1] FALSE

months_to_payoff(balance=5000, monthly_payment=100, apr=0.22)
#> 136.77905405676339

#>  payment  months  years     paid  interest

With the balance in A2, the monthly payment in B2, and the APR in C2 (as a decimal), NPER() solves for the number of months:
=NPER(C2/12, -B2, A2)

title: Managing Debt
section: 4 Total Interest Over a Loan’s Life
text:
4 Total Interest Over a Loan’s Life
For any installment loan (car, mortgage, student loan), the real cost is everything you pay minus what you borrowed.
Formula: Total Interest = (Monthly Payment × Number of Payments) − Loan Principal
Example: a $30,000 car loan at 7%. Over 6 years ($512 a month) you pay $6,864 in interest. Over 4 years ($719 a month) you pay $4,512. The shorter term saves $2,352.





$30,000 car loan: principal vs. interest for 6-year and 4-year terms







$30,000 car loan: principal vs. interest for 6-year and 4-year terms




The book rounds the payments to whole dollars. The exact payments are $511.47 and $718.39, so the exact interest is a few dollars lower. Each extra year on the loan adds interest, but the monthly payment drops less than you might expect.

RPythonExcel




show/hide
total_interest <- function(monthly_payment, n_months, principal) {
  (monthly_payment * n_months) - principal
}

# 6-year car loan vs. 4-year, $30,000 principal
total_interest(monthly_payment = 512, n_months = 72, principal = 30000)
#> [1] 6864
total_interest(monthly_payment = 719, n_months = 48, principal = 30000)
#> [1] 4512


Where do $512 and $719 come from? The standard loan payment formula, run here over four terms:


show/hide
loan_payment <- function(principal, annual_rate, years) {
  r <- annual_rate / 12
  n <- years * 12
  principal * r * (1 + r)^n / ((1 + r)^n - 1)
}

years <- 3:6
pmts  <- loan_payment(principal = 30000, annual_rate = 0.07, years = years)
data.frame(
  years    = years,
  payment  = fmt_dollar(pmts),
  interest = fmt_dollar(total_interest(pmts, years * 12, 30000), 0)
)
#> # A tibble: 4 × 3
#>   years payment interest
#>   <int> <chr>   <chr>   
#> 1     3 $926.31 $3,347  
#> 2     4 $718.39 $4,483  
#> 3     5 $594.04 $5,642  
#> 4     6 $511.47 $6,826






show/hide
def total_interest(monthly_payment, n_months, principal):
    return (monthly_payment * n_months) - principal

# 6-year car loan vs. 4-year, $30,000 principal
print(total_interest(monthly_payment=512, n_months=72, principal=30000))
#> 6864
print(total_interest(monthly_payment=719, n_months=48, principal=30000))
#> 4512


Where do $512 and $719 come from? The standard loan payment formula, run here over four terms:


show/hide
def loan_payment(principal, annual_rate, years):
    r = annual_rate / 12
    n = years * 12
    return principal * r * (1 + r) ** n / ((1 + r) ** n - 1)

for years in range(3, 7):
    pmt = loan_payment(principal=30000, annual_rate=0.07, years=years)
    print(f"{years} years: ${pmt:,.2f}/month, "
          f"${total_interest(pmt, years * 12, 30000):,.0f} interest")
#> 3 years: $926.31/month, $3,347 interest
#> 4 years: $718.39/month, $4,483 interest
#> 5 years: $594.04/month, $5,642 interest
#> 6 years: $511.47/month, $6,826 interest




With the monthly payment in A2, the number of months in B2, and the principal in C2:
=A2*B2-C2
To get the payment itself from a rate in D2 (as a decimal):
=-PMT(D2/12, B2, C2)
CUMIPMT() returns total interest in one step (as a negative number):
=-CUMIPMT(D2/12, B2, C2, 1, B2, 0)

section: 5 Student Loan to Income & Standard Payment
text:
5 Student Loan to Income & Standard Payment
The 1× rule says your student loans should not be bigger than your expected first year salary. Two numbers check it: the loan to income ratio, and the monthly payment that loan creates on a standard 10 year plan.
Formula: Loan to income ratio = Total loans ÷ Expected salary, and Monthly payment = Loan × r(1 + r)^n ÷ ((1 + r)^n − 1), where r = yearly rate ÷ 12 and n = 120 payments
Example: $45,000 ÷ $42,000 = about 1.07×, and the standard payment at 6.5% is about $511 a month.





$45,000 in student loans vs. a $42,000 starting salary







$45,000 in student loans vs. a $42,000 starting salary




A ratio above 1.0 means the loan bar runs past the salary line. At exactly 1×, every dollar borrowed costs about $0.0114 a month, so the payment is about 14% of gross pay no matter the major. What changes is how many dollars are left over.

RPythonExcel

  loan_total / expected_salary
}

  r <- annual_rate / 12
  n <- years * 12
  principal * (r * (1 + r)^n) / ((1 + r)^n - 1)
}

# $45,000 in loans, $42,000 expected starting salary
loan_income_ratio(loan_total = 45000, expected_salary = 42000)
#> [1] 1.071429

# standard 10-year monthly payment on that $45,000
monthly_standard_payment(principal = 45000)
#> [1] 510.9659

title: Managing Debt
text:
6 Income Driven Repayment Monthly Payment
Federal IDR plans protect part of your income and charge a percentage of the rest (your discretionary income).
Formula: Monthly payment = (AGI − threshold × Federal Poverty Guideline) × payment rate ÷ 12
Example (IBR): ($50,000 − 1.5 × $15,650) × 10% ÷ 12 = about $221 a month. For IBR loans from before July 2014 (15% rate), it is about $332.





$50,000 AGI under IBR: protected income, discretionary income, and the yearly payment







$50,000 AGI under IBR: protected income, discretionary income, and the yearly payment




If your AGI is below the protected amount, the payment is $0. Each extra $1,000 of income above that line adds only about $8 a month under IBR. SAVE used the same formula with a 225% threshold and a 5% undergraduate rate, but it ended in March 2026. RAP uses a sliding share of total AGI instead, so this function does not cover it.

RPythonExcel




show/hide
idr_monthly_payment <- function(agi,
                                poverty_guideline = 15650,
                                threshold_pct     = 1.5,
                                payment_rate      = 0.10) {
  discretionary <- max(0, agi - poverty_guideline * threshold_pct)
  round((discretionary * payment_rate) / 12, 2)
}

# IBR: $50,000 AGI, 150% FPG threshold, 10% rate
idr_monthly_payment(agi = 50000)
#> [1] 221.04

# IBR for loans before July 2014: 15% rate
idr_monthly_payment(agi = 50000, payment_rate = 0.15)
#> [1] 331.56


max() is not vectorized, so use sapply() to compare several incomes. The SAVE column is for history only.


show/hide
agis <- c(20000, 35000, 50000, 75000, 100000)
data.frame(
  agi       = fmt_dollar(agis, 0),
  ibr_new   = sapply(agis, idr_monthly_payment),
  ibr_old   = sapply(agis, idr_monthly_payment, payment_rate = 0.15),
  save_undg = sapply(agis, idr_monthly_payment, threshold_pct = 2.25, payment_rate = 0.05)
)

#> 3 $50,000    221.     332.      61.6
#> 4 $75,000    429.     644.     166.

title: Managing Debt
text:
7 Debt to Income Ratio (DTI)
Lenders calculate this about you. Calculate it yourself first.
Formula: DTI = (Total Monthly Debt Payments ÷ Gross Monthly Income) × 100
Example: $2,500 in debt payments on $7,000 gross income is about 36% DTI.
Benchmarks: below 20% healthy; 20 to 35% manageable; 36 to 43% stretched; above 43% danger zone (most mortgage lenders say no).





$7,000 monthly income split into debt payments and remaining income







$7,000 monthly income split into debt payments and remaining income




DTI uses gross pay (before taxes), so it looks smaller than how it feels. At about 36%, this borrower sits right on the line between manageable and stretched. Paying off one $400 car payment would bring them to about 30%.

RPythonExcel




show/hide
dti_ratio <- function(monthly_debt_payments, gross_monthly_income) {
  (monthly_debt_payments / gross_monthly_income) * 100
}

# $2,500 in debt payments on $7,000 gross income
dti_ratio(monthly_debt_payments = 2500, gross_monthly_income = 7000)
#> [1] 35.71429


Several scenarios, labeled with the book’s benchmarks:


show/hide
debts <- c(1000, 1750, 2500, 2800, 3200)
dti   <- dti_ratio(debts, gross_monthly_income = 7000)
data.frame(
  debt_payments = fmt_dollar(debts, 0),
  dti           = round(dti, 1),
  band          = cut(dti, breaks = c(-Inf, 20, 36, 43, Inf), right = FALSE,
                      labels = c("Healthy", "Manageable", "Stretched", "Danger zone"))
)

#>   debt_payments   dti band       
#>   <chr>         <dbl> <fct>      
#> 1 $1,000         14.3 Healthy    
#> 2 $1,750         25   Manageable 
#> 3 $2,500         35.7 Manageable 
#> 4 $2,800         40   Stretched  
#> 5 $3,200         45.7 Danger zone

title: Managing Debt
text:
8 Pay Off vs. Invest Comparison
Should extra money go to the loan or to investments? Compare the two rates.
Formula: Yearly edge of investing = Expected after tax investment return − After tax loan interest rate
A positive answer favors investing. A negative answer favors paying off the debt.
Example: a 5% mortgage vs. an expected 7% return. 7% − 5% = 2%, so the math favors investing by about 2% a year. But the 5% is guaranteed and the 7% is not.





Guaranteed 5% debt payoff vs. expected 7% investment return







Guaranteed 5% debt payoff vs. expected 7% investment return




A 2% edge sounds small, but it compounds. On $10,000 over 10 years, it is the gap between about $16,300 (the guaranteed path) and about $19,700 (the expected path). The book’s rule of thumb also adds a middle zone: between 4% and 6%, do both.

RPythonExcel




show/hide
payoff_vs_invest <- function(loan_rate, expected_return) {
  if (loan_rate > expected_return) {
    "Pay off the debt"
  } else if (loan_rate < expected_return) {
    "Invest the difference"
  } else {
    "Roughly a wash; do both"
  }
}

# 5% mortgage vs. expected 7% return
payoff_vs_invest(loan_rate = 0.05, expected_return = 0.07)
#> [1] "Invest the difference"


Several loan rates against the same 7% expected return, plus what $10,000 becomes in 10 years either way:

data.frame(
  loan_rate   = fmt_pct(loan_rates),
  edge        = fmt_pct(0.07 - loan_rates),
  decision    = sapply(loan_rates, payoff_vs_invest, expected_return = 0.07),
  payoff_path = fmt_dollar(10000 * (1 + loan_rates)^10, 0),
  invest_path = fmt_dollar(10000 * 1.07^10, 0)
)

#> 4 9%        -2%   Pay off… $23,674     $19,672    
#> 5 22%       -15%  Pay off… $73,046     $19,672

title: Managing Debt
text:
9 Avalanche vs. Snowball Math
Two ways to order several debts. Avalanche pays the highest APR first and saves the most. Snowball pays the smallest balance first and builds momentum.
Formula: Monthly interest saved by an extra payment = Extra payment × APR ÷ 12
Example: an extra $100 on Card B (24%) saves $2.00 of interest next month. The same $100 on Card A (18%) saves $1.50.





Avalanche order (highest APR first) vs. snowball order (smallest balance first)







Avalanche order (highest APR first) vs. snowball order (smallest balance first)




The book says to find the cost of snowball with a payoff calculator. The extra code below is a small one. It pays every minimum, sends the rest of a fixed monthly budget to the target debt, and rolls each freed up payment onto the next debt. The difference in total interest is the price of the snowball’s quick early wins. With these three cards, snowball costs about $338 more and takes one extra month.

RPythonExcel




show/hide
# avalanche: highest APR first
order_avalanche <- function(debts) {
  debts[order(-debts$apr), ]
}

# snowball: smallest balance first
order_snowball <- function(debts) {
  debts[order(debts$balance), ]
}

# your debts, as a small table
debts <- data.frame(
  name    = c("Card A", "Card B", "Card C"),
  balance = c(1000, 5000, 2000),
  apr     = c(0.18, 0.24, 0.15)
)

order_avalanche(debts)
#> # A tibble: 3 × 3
#>   name   balance   apr

payoff_sim <- function(debts, budget, order_fn) {

  interest <- 0

    bal      <- bal + int

    bal      <- bal - pay
    extra    <- budget - sum(pay)

10 Credit Utilization Ratio
How much of your available credit you are using. High use signals stress to credit scoring models.
Formula: Utilization = (Current Balance ÷ Credit Limit) × 100
Keep it under 30% on each card and across all cards. Under 10% is ideal.
Example: a $3,000 balance on a $10,000 limit is 30% utilization, right at the threshold.

title: Automating Savings
text:
Why automation matters: willpower is finite; save first and spend what remains (Sethi’s Conscious Spending Plan)
Money flow: split each paycheck on the first business day into savings, retirement, and checking
Method 1, direct deposit split: the cleanest approach; savings leave the paycheck before it reaches checking
Method 2, automatic bank transfers: the fallback; schedule a recurring transfer for the day after payday, never on payday itself
Pay yourself first math: Monthly Savings = Gross Monthly Income × Savings Rate, often split across an emergency fund, 401(k) match, sinking funds, and investing
Escalation: save half of every raise (Save More Tomorrow); stepping from 15% to 30% over seven years roughly doubles where you end up
Troubleshooting: lower the amount if you keep pulling money back; automate a percentage of average income if pay varies

title: Automating Savings
text:
3 Direct Deposit Split
The book’s Method 1 example: a $5,000 gross paycheck, a 25% savings goal, a 10% 401(k) contribution taken before taxes, and about $750 in taxes. The 401(k) already covers part of the goal, so the HYSA only needs the rest.
Formula: HYSA Split = (Gross × Savings Rate) − 401(k); Checking Split = Gross − 401(k) − Taxes − HYSA Split
Example: 401(k) = $500, so the HYSA split is $1,250 − $500 = $750. The deposit is $5,000 − $500 − $750 = $3,750, and checking gets $3,750 − $750 = $3,000.





Where a $5,000 gross paycheck goes with a direct deposit split







Where a $5,000 gross paycheck goes with a direct deposit split





RPythonExcel


deposit_split() returns each piece of the paycheck. pmax() keeps the HYSA split from going negative when the 401(k) alone meets the goal.


show/hide
deposit_split <- function(gross, savings_rate, k401_rate, taxes) {
  k401     <- gross * k401_rate
  hysa     <- pmax(gross * savings_rate - k401, 0)
  deposit  <- gross - k401 - taxes
  checking <- deposit - hysa
  data.frame(k401, taxes, deposit, hysa, checking)
}

split <- deposit_split(gross = 5000, savings_rate = 0.25, k401_rate = 0.10, taxes = 750)
split
#> # A tibble: 1 × 5
#>    k401 taxes deposit  hysa checking
#>   <dbl> <dbl>   <dbl> <dbl>    <dbl>
#> 1   500   750    3750   750     3000


Two checks: the pieces add back to the gross paycheck, and the total saved is 25% of gross.


show/hide
with(split, k401 + taxes + hysa + checking)
#> [1] 5000
with(split, (k401 + hysa) / 5000)
#> [1] 0.25


Different 401(k) rates change how much goes to the HYSA. Taxes are held at $750 to keep the comparison simple (in real life a bigger 401(k) lowers them). At 30% the 401(k) covers the whole goal, so the HYSA split is zero.


show/hide
do.call(rbind, lapply(c(0.05, 0.10, 0.15, 0.30), function(k) {
  cbind(k401_rate = k, deposit_split(5000, 0.25, k, taxes = 750))
}))

#>   k401_rate  k401 taxes deposit  hysa checking
#>       <dbl> <dbl> <dbl>   <dbl> <dbl>    <dbl>
#> 1      0.05   250   750    4000  1000     3000
#> 2      0.1    500   750    3750   750     3000
#> 3      0.15   750   750    3500   500     3000
#> 4      0.3   1500   750    2750     0     2750

def deposit_split(gross, savings_rate, k401_rate, taxes):
    k401 = gross * k401_rate
    hysa = max(gross * savings_rate - k401, 0)
    deposit = gross - k401 - taxes
    return {"k401": k401, "taxes": taxes, "deposit": deposit,
            "hysa": hysa, "checking": deposit - hysa}

print(split)
#> {'k401': 500.0, 'taxes': 750, 'deposit': 3750.0, 'hysa': 750.0, 'checking': 3000.0}


Check that the pieces add back to the gross paycheck and that 25% is saved.


show/hide
print(split["k401"] + split["taxes"] + split["hysa"] + split["checking"])
#> 5000.0
print((split["k401"] + split["hysa"]) / 5000)
#> 0.25


Try different 401(k) rates, holding taxes at $750 for simplicity. At 30% the HYSA split drops to zero.


show/hide
for k in [0.05, 0.10, 0.15, 0.30]:
    s = deposit_split(5000, 0.25, k, taxes=750)
    print(f"401(k) {k:4.0%}: HYSA ${s['hysa']:>5,.0f}  checking ${s['checking']:>6,.0f}")
#> 401(k)   5%: HYSA $1,000  checking $ 3,000
#> 401(k)  10%: HYSA $  750  checking $ 3,000
#> 401(k)  15%: HYSA $  500  checking $ 3,000
#> 401(k)  30%: HYSA $    0  checking $ 2,750




Assuming Gross is in B2, Savings_Rate in C2, 401k_Rate in D2, and Taxes in E2:
401(k) (F2):    =B2 * D2
HYSA (G2):      =MAX(B2 * C2 - F2, 0)
Checking (H2):  =B2 - F2 - E2 - G2



How to read this result: the HYSA and checking numbers are what you type into your payroll portal. The 401(k) and taxes are handled by payroll before the deposit.

text:
4 Escalating with Raises
Save half of every raise. Your spending still grows a little, and your savings rate climbs without a budget cut.
Formula: Extra Monthly Savings = (New Income − Old Income) × 0.5 ÷ 12; 30 Year Value = Monthly × ((1 + r/12)^360 − 1) ÷ (r/12)
Example: a raise from $50,000 to $52,000 adds $1,000 a year ($83.33 a month) to savings. In the book’s escalation table, $625 a month at 7% for 30 years grows to about $762k, and $1,575 a month grows to about $1.92M.





30 years of saving each year’s monthly amount at a 7% return







30 years of saving each year’s monthly amount at a 7% return





RPythonExcel


raise_to_savings() returns the extra monthly savings from a raise.

}

  monthly * ((1 + r)^(12 * years) - 1) / r
}

title: High-Yield Savings Accounts
text:
Separate account: the real benefit of a savings account at a different bank is friction; 1 to 2 days to move money back stops impulse spending
Choosing an account: need it within 6 months? Use a HYSA. Can you lock it away for 3 to 60 months? Consider a CD

Savings hierarchy: emergency fund, sinking funds, and short term goals go in a HYSA; 3 to 5 year goals in CDs or short term bonds; 5+ years goes to investing

text:
2 HYSA Balance
APY is the total return for a year with compounding already included. To grow a balance, multiply by (1 + APY) once for each year you hold the money.
Formula: Ending Balance = Starting Balance × (1 + APY)^years
(The daily math belongs to the APR: APY = (1 + APR ÷ 365)^365 − 1.)
Example: $10,000 at 4.35% APY grows to $10,000 × 1.0435 = $10,435 after one year ($435 in interest) and to $12,373 after five years.





$10,000 at 4.35% APY: deposit and interest earned, year by year







$10,000 at 4.35% APY: deposit and interest earned, year by year





RPythonExcel


hysa_balance() grows a deposit at the APY for a given number of years.


show/hide

  principal * (1 + annual_apy)^years
}

hysa_balance(principal = 10000, annual_apy = 0.0435, years = 1)
#> [1] 10435

# Same money after 5 years
hysa_balance(principal = 10000, annual_apy = 0.0435, years = 5)
#> [1] 12372.64

title: High-Yield Savings Accounts
text:
3 Small Rate Gaps Over Time
The book says a 0.3% difference looks like noise at first but adds up over 30 years of regular deposits. To check, we need the growth of a monthly deposit, using the monthly rate that matches the APY.
Formula: Future Value = Deposit × ((1 + i)^(12 × years) − 1) ÷ i, where i = (1 + APY)^(1/12) − 1
Example: $500 a month for 30 years grows to about $342,635 at 4.0% APY and $360,801 at 4.3% APY, a gap of about $18,166.





$500 a month for 30 years at three APYs







$500 a month for 30 years at three APYs

hysa_deposits_fv() grows a fixed monthly deposit at a given APY.

hysa_deposits_fv <- function(monthly_deposit, annual_apy, years) {
  i <- (1 + annual_apy)^(1 / 12) - 1

}

round(fv)

round(diff(fv))
#> [1] 18166

Assuming Monthly_Deposit is in cell B2, Annual_APY is in cell C2, and Years is in cell D2:
=FV((1 + C2) ^ (1 / 12) - 1, D2 * 12, -B2)
Put the second APY in C3, then the gap in E2:
=FV((1 + C3) ^ (1 / 12) - 1, D2 * 12, -B2) - FV((1 + C2) ^ (1 / 12) - 1, D2 * 12, -B2)



How to read this result: the gap is small for the first few years and grows with time. It is worth picking a good rate once, but not worth switching banks every month to chase 0.05%.

title: High-Yield Savings Accounts
text:
4 FDIC Coverage
FDIC insurance covers up to $250,000 per account holder per bank. Anything above that at one bank is not insured.
Formula: Insured = smaller of (Balance, $250,000); Uninsured = Balance − Insured; Banks Needed = Balance ÷ $250,000, rounded up
Example: a $10,000 balance is fully insured. A $500,000 balance at one bank has $250,000 uninsured, so it needs two banks.

RPythonExcel




show/hide
fdic_coverage <- function(balance, limit = 250000) {
  insured <- pmin(balance, limit)
  data.frame(
    balance      = balance,
    insured      = insured,
    uninsured    = balance - insured,
    banks_needed = ceiling(balance / limit)
  )
}

fdic_coverage(balance = c(10000, 250000, 500000, 610000))
#> # A tibble: 4 × 4
#>   balance insured uninsured banks_needed
#>     <dbl>   <dbl>     <dbl>        <dbl>
#> 1   10000   10000         0            1
#> 2  250000  250000         0            1
#> 3  500000  250000    250000            2
#> 4  610000  250000    360000            3


A balance of exactly $250,000 is fully covered and needs only one bank.




show/hide
import math

def fdic_coverage(balance, limit=250000):
    insured = min(balance, limit)
    return {
        "balance": balance,
        "insured": insured,
        "uninsured": balance - insured,
        "banks_needed": math.ceil(balance / limit),
    }

for balance in [10000, 250000, 500000, 610000]:
    print(fdic_coverage(balance))
#> {'balance': 10000, 'insured': 10000, 'uninsured': 0, 'banks_needed': 1}
#> {'balance': 250000, 'insured': 250000, 'uninsured': 0, 'banks_needed': 1}
#> {'balance': 500000, 'insured': 250000, 'uninsured': 250000, 'banks_needed': 2}
#> {'balance': 610000, 'insured': 250000, 'uninsured': 360000, 'banks_needed': 3}




Assuming Balance is in cell B2:
Insured (C2):       =MIN(B2, 250000)
Uninsured (D2):     =B2 - C2
Banks needed (E2):  =ROUNDUP(B2 / 250000, 0)



How to read this result: if the uninsured column is above zero, move that amount to an account at a different bank.

title: Index Funds
text:
What an index fund is: an index is a list of companies (like the S&P 500); an index fund buys everything on the list, weighted by company size (market cap), with no manager picking winners (passive vs. active)
Why index funds win: SPIVA shows 79% of large US active funds trailed the S&P 500 in 2025 and about 9 in 10 over 15 years; Bogle’s math says the average investor earns the market return minus costs
Expense ratios: a yearly fee taken out quietly; 0.04% vs. 1% is $4 vs. $100 on $10,000; look for funds under 0.10%
Total market vs. S&P 500 vs. international: the first two move almost together; experts disagree on how much international to hold (Bogle and Collins little or none, Felix anywhere from 10% to 60% home country)
ETFs vs. mutual funds: same holdings, different packaging; ETFs trade all day and are a little more tax efficient, mutual funds make automatic investing easier
How to pick one: go broad, check the expense ratio, look for “index” in the 401(k) list (or a target date fund), automate, and leave it alone

title: Index Funds
text:
2 The Fee This Year
Every year, the fund takes a slice of your balance as its fee.
Formula: Yearly fee = Balance × Expense ratio
Example: $10,000 × 0.0004 = $4. $10,000 × 0.01 = $100, or 25 times as much.





One year of fees on $10,000







One year of fees on $10,000




The second example uses a table of typical expense ratios across a few balances. The fee grows with your balance, so a fee that costs pocket change at $10,000 costs real money at $250,000.

RPythonExcel




show/hide
yearly_fee <- function(balance, expense_ratio) {
  balance * expense_ratio
}

# $10,000 in an index fund vs. an active fund
yearly_fee(balance = 10000, expense_ratio = c(0.0004, 0.01))
#> [1]   4 100

# several funds across several balances
ratios   <- c(index = 0.0004, target_date = 0.0010, active = 0.01)
balances <- c(10000, 50000, 250000)
fees <- outer(balances, ratios, yearly_fee)
data.frame(balance = balances, fees)
#> # A tibble: 3 × 4
#>   balance index target_date active
#>     <dbl> <dbl>       <dbl>  <dbl>
#> 1   10000     4          10    100
#> 2   50000    20          50    500
#> 3  250000   100         250   2500

# sanity check: how many times as expensive?
0.01 / 0.0004
#> [1] 25

import numpy as np

def yearly_fee(balance, expense_ratio):
    return balance * expense_ratio

# $10,000 in an index fund vs. an active fund
print(yearly_fee(balance=10000, expense_ratio=np.array([0.0004, 0.01])))
#> [  4. 100.]

# several funds across several balances
ratios = {"index": 0.0004, "target_date": 0.0010, "active": 0.01}
for bal in [10000, 50000, 250000]:
    fees = ", ".join(f"{k} ${yearly_fee(bal, v):,.0f}" for k, v in ratios.items())
    print(f"${bal:,}: {fees}")
#> $10,000: index $4, target_date $10, active $100
#> $50,000: index $20, target_date $50, active $500
