With Balance in B2 and Expense ratio in C2:
=B2 * C2
For a table, put balances down column A (A3:A5) and ratios across row 2 (B2:D2), then fill B3 across and down:
=$A3 * B$2



Read the fee as dollars you never see. The active fund costs $2,500 a year on $250,000, and the index fund costs $100.

title: Index Funds
section: 3 What Fees Cost Over a Lifetime
text:
3 What Fees Cost Over a Lifetime
The fee comes out of the return, so subtract it from the return before you compound.
Formula: FV = PMT × [((1 + r)^n − 1) ÷ r], where r = (return − expense ratio) ÷ 12
Example: $300/month for 40 years at 7%. The index fund (0.04%) grows to about $778,655 and the active fund (1%) to about $597,447. Both people put in the same $144,000. The 1% fee cost $181,207, about 23% of what the index fund investor ended up with.





$300/month at 7%, with a 0.04% fee vs. a 1% fee







$300/month at 7%, with a 0.04% fee vs. a 1% fee




The second example tries several expense ratios over 40 years and reports the share of the low cost result each one loses. The edge case is a 0% fee, which is just the plain annuity from Investing Basics.

RPythonExcel




show/hide
future_value_after_fees <- function(contribution, annual_return, expense_ratio, years) {
  rate    <- (annual_return - expense_ratio) / 12
  periods <- years * 12
  contribution * (((1 + rate)^periods - 1) / rate)
}

# $300/month for 40 years at 7%, index fund vs. active fund
index_fund  <- future_value_after_fees(300, 0.07, 0.0004, 40)
active_fund <- future_value_after_fees(300, 0.07, 0.01, 40)
c(index_fund = index_fund, active_fund = active_fund,
  cost_of_fees = index_fund - active_fund)
#>   index_fund  active_fund cost_of_fees 
#>     778654.7     597447.2     181207.5

# share of the index fund result lost to the 1% fee
(index_fund - active_fund) / index_fund
#> [1] 0.2327187

# several expense ratios over 40 years
er <- c(0, 0.0004, 0.001, 0.005, 0.01, 0.015)
fv <- future_value_after_fees(300, 0.07, er, 40)
data.frame(
  expense_ratio_pct = er * 100,
  ending_balance    = round(fv),
  lost_vs_index_pct = round(100 * (1 - fv / index_fund), 1)
)
#> # A tibble: 6 × 3
#>   expense_ratio_pct ending_balance
#>               <dbl>          <dbl>
#> 1              0            787444
#> 2              0.04         778655
#> 3              0.1          765675
#> 4              0.5          685086
#> 5              1            597447
#> 6              1.5          522312
#> # ℹ 1 more variable: lost_vs_index_pct <dbl>






show/hide
import numpy as np

def future_value_after_fees(contribution, annual_return, expense_ratio, years):
    rate = (annual_return - expense_ratio) / 12
    periods = years * 12
    return contribution * (((1 + rate) ** periods - 1) / rate)

# $300/month for 40 years at 7%, index fund vs. active fund
index_fund = future_value_after_fees(300, 0.07, 0.0004, 40)
active_fund = future_value_after_fees(300, 0.07, 0.01, 40)
print(round(index_fund), round(active_fund), round(index_fund - active_fund))
#> 778655 597447 181207

# share of the index fund result lost to the 1% fee
print((index_fund - active_fund) / index_fund)
#> 0.23271867146818886

# several expense ratios over 40 years
er = np.array([0, 0.0004, 0.001, 0.005, 0.01, 0.015])
fv = future_value_after_fees(300, 0.07, er, 40)
for e, v in zip(er, fv):
    print(f"{e:.2%}: ${v:,.0f} ({1 - v / index_fund:+.1%} vs. index)")
#> 0.00%: $787,444 (-1.1% vs. index)
#> 0.04%: $778,655 (+0.0% vs. index)
#> 0.10%: $765,675 (+1.7% vs. index)
#> 0.50%: $685,086 (+12.0% vs. index)
#> 1.00%: $597,447 (+23.3% vs. index)
#> 1.50%: $522,312 (+32.9% vs. index)




With Contribution in B2, Return in C2, Expense ratio in D2, and Years in E2:
=FV((C2 - D2) / 12, E2 * 12, -B2)
Copy the row down with different expense ratios in column D to build the comparison table.



Read the lifetime cost as a share, not a dollar amount. A 1% fee takes about 23% of the ending balance, which is why the book says close to a quarter. A negative “lost” number means that fund beat the 0.04% index fund (only possible here with a lower fee).

title: Estate Planning
text:
Why it matters young: at 18 your parents lose the right to act for you; set up a plan while you’re thinking clearly, since people tend to miss their own cognitive decline
Beneficiary designations: the ten minute task; name a primary and contingent beneficiary on retirement plans, IRAs, HSAs, life insurance, and bank (POD) and brokerage (TOD) accounts; these forms override your will
Financial power of attorney: a durable POA names an agent to handle your money if you can’t
Healthcare directive and HIPAA release: a healthcare proxy and living will (often one advance directive), plus a HIPAA form so doctors can share information
Will and trust: a will covers what has no beneficiary, names an executor, and names a guardian for children; without one, state intestate succession decides; most people starting out don’t need a trust
Paperwork and parents: store originals safely, keep an account list (no passwords), set up password manager emergency access, and ask your parents about their plan

section: 2 What You Own and What You Owe
text:
2 What You Own and What You Owe
Your estate starts with your net worth: everything you own minus everything you owe.
Formula: Net worth = Total assets − Total debts





Assets, debts, and net worth for a 25 year old







Assets, debts, and net worth for a 25 year old




Example: ($12,000 + $6,000 + $8,000 + $9,000) − ($6,000 + $1,000) = $35,000 − $7,000 = a net worth of $28,000.

RPythonExcel


net_worth() takes two named vectors, so you can see each item and the total.


show/hide
net_worth <- function(assets, debts) {
  sum(assets) - sum(debts)
}

assets <- c(k401 = 12000, roth_ira = 6000, savings = 8000, car = 9000)
debts  <- c(car_loan = 6000, credit_card = 1000)
net_worth(assets, debts)
#> [1] 28000


Sanity check: paying off the credit card from savings doesn’t change net worth. Cash goes down by $1,000 and so does debt.


show/hide
assets_after <- replace(assets, "savings", 8000 - 1000)
debts_after  <- replace(debts, "credit_card", 0)
net_worth(assets_after, debts_after)
#> [1] 28000


Edge case: net worth can be negative. A recent graduate with $3,000 in savings, a $5,000 car, and $30,000 in student loans starts below zero, and that’s common.


show/hide
net_worth(assets = c(savings = 3000, car = 5000),
          debts  = c(student_loans = 30000))
#> [1] -22000




net_worth() takes two dictionaries, so you can see each item and the total.


show/hide
def net_worth(assets, debts):
    return sum(assets.values()) - sum(debts.values())

assets = {"401k": 12000, "roth_ira": 6000, "savings": 8000, "car": 9000}
debts = {"car_loan": 6000, "credit_card": 1000}
print(net_worth(assets, debts))
#> 28000


Sanity check: paying off the credit card from savings doesn’t change net worth.


show/hide
assets_after = {**assets, "savings": 8000 - 1000}
debts_after = {**debts, "credit_card": 0}
print(net_worth(assets_after, debts_after))
#> 28000


Edge case: net worth can be negative.


show/hide
print(net_worth({"savings": 3000, "car": 5000}, {"student_loans": 30000}))
#> -22000




Assuming assets are listed in B2:B5 and debts in C2:C3:
=SUM(B2:B5) - SUM(C2:C3)



How to read this result: net worth is the yearly check in on your progress. It’s also roughly what your estate would be worth today, before adding any life insurance.

title: Estate Planning
section: 3 How Much Your Beneficiary Forms Control
text:
3 How Much Your Beneficiary Forms Control
Life insurance isn’t part of net worth while you’re alive, but it pays out when you die. Add it, then split the estate by what decides who gets each piece.
Formula: Share controlled by beneficiary forms = Assets with a named beneficiary ÷ Total estate





What decides who gets each part of the estate







What decides who gets each part of the estate




Example: ($12,000 + $6,000 + $45,000 + $8,000) ÷ $80,000 = about 89% of the estate, decided by forms that take minutes to fill out. That’s why beneficiary designations come before a will for most young people.

RPythonExcel


beneficiary_share() divides what the forms control by the whole estate.


show/hide
beneficiary_share <- function(with_beneficiary, without_beneficiary) {
  sum(with_beneficiary) / (sum(with_beneficiary) + sum(without_beneficiary))
}

with_beneficiary    <- c(k401 = 12000, roth_ira = 6000, life_insurance = 45000, savings_pod = 8000)
without_beneficiary <- c(car = 9000)
beneficiary_share(with_beneficiary, without_beneficiary)
#> [1] 0.8875


What if some forms are blank? A blank form moves that account into the “will or state law” pile. Each scenario below starts from the same $80,000 estate.


show/hide
all_assets <- c(k401 = 12000, roth_ira = 6000, life_insurance = 45000,
                savings = 8000, car = 9000)
scenarios <- list(
  "all forms filled"   = c("k401", "roth_ira", "life_insurance", "savings"),
  "no POD on savings"  = c("k401", "roth_ira", "life_insurance"),
  "only the 401(k)"    = c("k401"),
  "no forms at all"    = character(0)
)
data.frame(
  scenario     = names(scenarios),
  forms_share  = sapply(scenarios, function(s)
    beneficiary_share(all_assets[s], all_assets[!names(all_assets) %in% s])),
  through_will = sapply(scenarios, function(s) sum(all_assets[!names(all_assets) %in% s])),
  row.names    = NULL
)
#> # A tibble: 4 × 3
#>   scenario          forms_share through_will
#>   <chr>                   <dbl>        <dbl>
#> 1 all forms filled        0.888         9000
#> 2 no POD on savings       0.788        17000
#> 3 only the 401(k)         0.15         68000
#> 4 no forms at all         0            80000




beneficiary_share() divides what the forms control by the whole estate.


show/hide
def beneficiary_share(with_beneficiary, without_beneficiary):
    named = sum(with_beneficiary.values())
    return named / (named + sum(without_beneficiary.values()))

with_beneficiary = {"401k": 12000, "roth_ira": 6000, "life_insurance": 45000, "savings_pod": 8000}
without_beneficiary = {"car": 9000}
print(beneficiary_share(with_beneficiary, without_beneficiary))
#> 0.8875


What if some forms are blank?


show/hide
all_assets = {"401k": 12000, "roth_ira": 6000, "life_insurance": 45000,
              "savings": 8000, "car": 9000}
scenarios = {
    "all forms filled": ["401k", "roth_ira", "life_insurance", "savings"],
    "no POD on savings": ["401k", "roth_ira", "life_insurance"],
    "only the 401(k)": ["401k"],
    "no forms at all": [],
}
for name, named in scenarios.items():
    yes = {k: v for k, v in all_assets.items() if k in named}
    no = {k: v for k, v in all_assets.items() if k not in named}
    print(f"{name:<18} {beneficiary_share(yes, no):>5.0%}  through will: ${sum(no.values()):,}")

#> no POD on savings    79%  through will: $17,000
#> only the 401(k)      15%  through will: $68,000
#> no forms at all       0%  through will: $80,000

=SUM(B2:B5) / (SUM(B2:B5) + SUM(C2))
To test blank forms, list every asset in B2:B6 with Yes or No in C2:C6 for “has a beneficiary,” then:
=SUMIF(C2:C6, "Yes", B2:B6) / SUM(B2:B6)



How to read this result: the higher the share, the less your will has to do. With every form filled in, a will only decides the car. With no forms, all $80,000 goes through probate.

title: Investing Basics
section: 2 Future Value and the Rule of 72
text:
2 Future Value and the Rule of 72
Each year’s growth is applied to a bigger base, so the balance curves upward instead of rising in a straight line.
Formula: FV = PV × (1 + r)^n
Rule of 72: Years to double ≈ 72 ÷ annual return %
Example: $10,000 at 7% for 10 years grows to about $19,672, and at 7% money doubles roughly every 10 years.





$10,000 growing at 7%: value at each checkpoint







$10,000 growing at 7%: value at each checkpoint




The Rule of 72 is a shortcut. The exact doubling time is log(2) ÷ log(1 + r). The shortcut is very close for returns between about 4% and 12%, and drifts further off at the extremes.

RPythonExcel




show/hide
future_value <- function(present_value, rate, years) {
  present_value * (1 + rate)^years
}

rule_of_72 <- function(annual_return_pct) {
  72 / annual_return_pct
}

# $10,000 at 7% for 10 years
future_value(present_value = 10000, rate = 0.07, years = 10)
#> [1] 19671.51

# years to double at 7%
rule_of_72(annual_return_pct = 7)
#> [1] 10.28571

# the same $10,000 across several horizons (40 years matches the book's line chart)
data.frame(
  years = c(5, 10, 20, 30, 40),
  value = round(future_value(10000, 0.07, c(5, 10, 20, 30, 40)))
)
#> # A tibble: 5 × 2
#>   years  value
#>   <dbl>  <dbl>
#> 1     5  14026
#> 2    10  19672
#> 3    20  38697
#> 4    30  76123
#> 5    40 149745

# sanity check: Rule of 72 vs. the exact doubling time
rates <- c(0.02, 0.04, 0.07, 0.10, 0.15)
data.frame(
  return_pct = rates * 100,
  rule_of_72 = round(rule_of_72(rates * 100), 1),
  exact      = round(log(2) / log(1 + rates), 1)
)
#> # A tibble: 5 × 3
#>   return_pct rule_of_72 exact
#>        <dbl>      <dbl> <dbl>
#> 1          2       36    35  
#> 2          4       18    17.7
#> 3          7       10.3  10.2
#> 4         10        7.2   7.3
#> 5         15        4.8   5






show/hide
import numpy as np

def future_value(present_value, rate, years):
    return present_value * (1 + rate) ** years

def rule_of_72(annual_return_pct):
    return 72 / annual_return_pct

# $10,000 at 7% for 10 years
print(future_value(present_value=10000, rate=0.07, years=10))
#> 19671.513572895663

# years to double at 7%
print(rule_of_72(annual_return_pct=7))
#> 10.285714285714286

# the same $10,000 across several horizons
horizons = np.array([5, 10, 20, 30, 40])
print(np.round(future_value(10000, 0.07, horizons)))
#> [ 14026.  19672.  38697.  76123. 149745.]

# sanity check: Rule of 72 vs. the exact doubling time
rates = np.array([0.02, 0.04, 0.07, 0.10, 0.15])
for r, rule, exact in zip(rates, rule_of_72(rates * 100), np.log(2) / np.log(1 + rates)):
    print(f"{r:.0%}: rule {rule:.1f} yrs, exact {exact:.1f} yrs")
#> 2%: rule 36.0 yrs, exact 35.0 yrs
#> 4%: rule 18.0 yrs, exact 17.7 yrs
#> 7%: rule 10.3 yrs, exact 10.2 yrs
#> 10%: rule 7.2 yrs, exact 7.3 yrs
#> 15%: rule 4.8 yrs, exact 5.0 yrs




With present value in A2, rate in B2 (as a decimal), and years in C2:
=A2*(1+B2)^C2
The built-in function gives the same number:
=FV(B2, C2, 0, -A2)
Rule of 72 with the return as a whole number (7) in E2, and the exact doubling time with the decimal rate in B2:
=72/E2
=NPER(B2, 0, -1, 2)
List several horizons down column C and copy the first formula down to compare them.



Read the result as “what one deposit becomes if you leave it alone.” At 7%, the Rule of 72 says 10.3 years and the exact answer is 10.2 years, so the shortcut is good enough for planning.

title: Investing Basics
text:
3 Future Value of Regular Contributions
Investing a fixed amount every month builds wealth two ways: the money you put in, and the growth on everything you put in before.
Formula: FV = PMT × [((1 + r)^n − 1) ÷ r]
Example: $500/month for 30 years (360 months) at a 7% annual return (about 0.583% per month) grows to about $610,000, and only $180,000 of that is money you put in.





$500/month contributions at 7%: contributed vs. gains







$500/month contributions at 7%: contributed vs. gains




Starting earlier matters more than putting in more. The second example compares the same $500/month started at 25, 35, and 45, all ending at 65. The book’s recap number ($50/month for 30 years is about $61,000) is the same math at one tenth the size.

RPythonExcel




show/hide
future_value_series <- function(contribution, rate, periods) {
  contribution * (((1 + rate)^periods - 1) / rate)
}

# $500/month for 30 years at a 7% annual return (monthly rate = 0.07 / 12)
future_value_series(contribution = 500, rate = 0.07 / 12, periods = 30 * 12)
#> [1] 609985.5

# the recap example: $50/month for 30 years
future_value_series(contribution = 50, rate = 0.07 / 12, periods = 30 * 12)
#> [1] 60998.55

# start age comparison: $500/month until 65
start_age <- c(25, 35, 45)
years     <- 65 - start_age
total     <- future_value_series(500, 0.07 / 12, years * 12)
data.frame(
  start_age,
  years,
  contributed = 500 * 12 * years,
  total       = round(total),
  pct_growth  = round(100 * (1 - (500 * 12 * years) / total))
)
#> # A tibble: 3 × 5
#>   start_age years contributed   total pct_growth
#>       <dbl> <dbl>       <dbl>   <dbl>      <dbl>
#> 1        25    40      240000 1312407         82
#> 2        35    30      180000  609985         70
#> 3        45    20      120000  260463         54






show/hide
import numpy as np

def future_value_series(contribution, rate, periods):
    return contribution * (((1 + rate) ** periods - 1) / rate)

# $500/month for 30 years at a 7% annual return
print(future_value_series(contribution=500, rate=0.07 / 12, periods=30 * 12))
#> 609985.4978879723

# the recap example: $50/month for 30 years
print(future_value_series(contribution=50, rate=0.07 / 12, periods=30 * 12))
#> 60998.54978879723

# start age comparison: $500/month until 65
start_age = np.array([25, 35, 45])
years = 65 - start_age
total = future_value_series(500, 0.07 / 12, years * 12)
contributed = 500 * 12 * years
for a, c, t in zip(start_age, contributed, total):
    print(f"start {a}: put in ${c:,.0f}, ends with ${t:,.0f} ({1 - c / t:.0%} growth)")
#> start 25: put in $240,000, ends with $1,312,407 (82% growth)
#> start 35: put in $180,000, ends with $609,985 (70% growth)
#> start 45: put in $120,000, ends with $260,463 (54% growth)




With the monthly contribution in A2, the annual rate in B2 (as a decimal), and the number of years in C2:
=A2*(((1+B2/12)^(C2*12)-1)/(B2/12))
The built-in FV() function gives the same answer:
=FV(B2/12, C2*12, -A2)
Money contributed is =A2*12*C2; subtract it from the FV() result to get the growth.



Read the result as two layers. At 30 years, about 70% of the $610,000 is growth, not deposits. Starting at 25 instead of 45 more than quadruples the ending balance while only doubling what you put in.

title: Investing Basics
text:
4 Real (Inflation-Adjusted) Return
Inflation shrinks what each dollar buys, so the return that matters is what’s left after inflation.
Formula: Real Return = (1 + nominal) ÷ (1 + inflation) − 1
Example: (1.07 ÷ 1.03) − 1 = about 3.88%, a little less than the 4% you’d get by simple subtraction.





Nominal return, inflation, and real return







Nominal return, inflation, and real return




The second example compares several investments against 3% inflation. Cash earning 4% (one of the book’s common mistakes) barely beats inflation, and cash earning less than inflation has a negative real return. The last line shows what $76,123 (the book’s 30 year example) is worth in today’s dollars.

RPythonExcel




show/hide
real_return <- function(nominal, inflation) {
  (1 + nominal) / (1 + inflation) - 1
}

# 7% nominal return against 3% inflation
real_return(nominal = 0.07, inflation = 0.03)
#> [1] 0.03883495

# several investments against 3% inflation
data.frame(
  investment  = c("Cash (1%)", "High yield savings (4%)", "60/40 (7%)", "Stocks (10%)"),
  nominal     = c(0.01, 0.04, 0.07, 0.10),
  simple      = c(0.01, 0.04, 0.07, 0.10) - 0.03,
  real        = round(real_return(c(0.01, 0.04, 0.07, 0.10), 0.03), 4)
)
#> # A tibble: 4 × 4
#>   investment              nominal simple    real
#>   <chr>                     <dbl>  <dbl>   <dbl>
#> 1 Cash (1%)                  0.01  -0.02 -0.0194
#> 2 High yield savings (4%)    0.04   0.01  0.0097
#> 3 60/40 (7%)                 0.07   0.04  0.0388
#> 4 Stocks (10%)               0.1    0.07  0.068

# $10,000 at 7% for 30 years, in today's dollars
10000 * 1.07^30 / 1.03^30
#> [1] 31361.48
10000 * (1 + real_return(0.07, 0.03))^30
#> [1] 31361.48






show/hide
def real_return(nominal, inflation):
    return (1 + nominal) / (1 + inflation) - 1

# 7% nominal return against 3% inflation
print(real_return(nominal=0.07, inflation=0.03))
#> 0.03883495145631066

# several investments against 3% inflation
for name, nominal in [("Cash", 0.01), ("High yield savings", 0.04),
                      ("60/40", 0.07), ("Stocks", 0.10)]:
    print(f"{name} ({nominal:.0%}): simple {nominal - 0.03:.2%}, real {real_return(nominal, 0.03):.2%}")
#> Cash (1%): simple -2.00%, real -1.94%
#> High yield savings (4%): simple 1.00%, real 0.97%
#> 60/40 (7%): simple 4.00%, real 3.88%
#> Stocks (10%): simple 7.00%, real 6.80%

# $10,000 at 7% for 30 years, in today's dollars
print(10000 * 1.07 ** 30 / 1.03 ** 30)
#> 31361.482876349524




With nominal return in A2 and inflation in B2 (both as decimals):
=(1+A2)/(1+B2)-1
To turn a future balance in C2 into today’s dollars over D2 years:
=C2/(1+B2)^D2



Read a negative real return as “losing buying power, even though the balance went up.” The $76,123 in 30 years buys about what $31,400 buys today, which is why the book says to think in real terms.

title: Major Purchases
text:
Renting vs. buying: “renting is throwing money away” is a myth; you pay for shelter either way, and Ben Felix’s research shows renting and investing the difference often matches or beats owning
True cost of owning: mortgage interest, property tax (1% to 2%), maintenance (about 1%), insurance, closing costs (3% to 5%), and the opportunity cost of the down payment
Felix’s 5% rule: unrecoverable costs run about 5% of home value per year (property tax ~1% + maintenance ~1% + cost of capital ~3%); divide by 12 and compare to rent
When to buy or rent: buy if you’ll stay 7+ years, have stable income and an emergency fund, and keep housing under 28% to 30% of gross income; rent if you may move within 5 to 7 years or need flexibility; a decision flowchart ties it together
Front loaded interest: on a 30 year mortgage at 6%, more than 80% of the first year’s payments go to interest, so moving every 5 years means barely touching principal

title: Major Purchases
text:
2 The Rent-vs-Buy 5% Rule
The 5% rule adds up three costs every owner pays and never gets back. Divide by 12 and you have a monthly rent to compare against.
Formula: Monthly cost of owning ≈ (Home Value × 0.05) ÷ 12





The three components of the 5% rule on a $500,000 home







The three components of the 5% rule on a $500,000 home




Example: a $500,000 home → (500,000 × 0.05) ÷ 12 = $2,083 a month. Rent below that, and renting and investing the difference tends to win.

RPythonExcel


rent_buy_threshold() turns the 5% rule into a monthly rent figure.


show/hide
rent_buy_threshold <- function(home_value, unrecoverable_rate = 0.05) {
  (home_value * unrecoverable_rate) / 12
}

# $500,000 home at the standard 5% unrecoverable rate
rent_buy_threshold(home_value = 500000)
#> [1] 2083.333


The 5% is a sum of parts. Splitting it shows which part drives the total.


show/hide
yearly <- 500000 * c(property_tax = 0.01, maintenance = 0.01, cost_of_capital = 0.03)
c(yearly, total = sum(yearly), monthly = sum(yearly) / 12)
#>    property_tax     maintenance cost_of_capital 
#>        5000.000        5000.000       15000.000 
#>           total         monthly 
#>       25000.000        2083.333


Compare several homes to a $2,000 rent. The function works on a whole vector of prices at once.


show/hide
homes <- data.frame(home_value = c(300000L, 400000L, 500000L, 600000L))
homes$threshold <- round(rent_buy_threshold(homes$home_value))
homes$rent      <- 2000
homes$verdict   <- ifelse(homes$rent < homes$threshold, "rent and invest", "buying competes")
homes

#>   home_value threshold  rent verdict        
#>        <int>     <dbl> <dbl> <chr>          
#> 1     300000      1250  2000 buying competes
#> 2     400000      1667  2000 buying competes
#> 3     500000      2083  2000 rent and invest
#> 4     600000      2500  2000 rent and invest


Edge case: the 3% cost of capital depends on interest rates and expected returns. In a low rate era a 4% total is closer; with high rates, 6% may fit better.


show/hide
round(sapply(c(0.04, 0.05, 0.06), rent_buy_threshold, home_value = 500000))
#> [1] 1667 2083 2500




rent_buy_threshold() turns the 5% rule into a monthly rent figure.


show/hide
def rent_buy_threshold(home_value, unrecoverable_rate=0.05):
    return (home_value * unrecoverable_rate) / 12

# $500,000 home at the standard 5% unrecoverable rate
print(rent_buy_threshold(home_value=500000))
#> 2083.3333333333335


The 5% split into its parts:


show/hide
parts = {"property_tax": 0.01, "maintenance": 0.01, "cost_of_capital": 0.03}
yearly = {k: 500000 * v for k, v in parts.items()}
print(yearly, "total:", sum(yearly.values()), "monthly:", round(sum(yearly.values()) / 12, 2))
#> {'property_tax': 5000.0, 'maintenance': 5000.0, 'cost_of_capital': 15000.0} total: 25000.0 monthly: 2083.33


Compare several homes to a $2,000 rent:


show/hide
rent = 2000
for home in [300000, 400000, 500000, 600000]:
    t = rent_buy_threshold(home)
    verdict = "rent and invest" if rent < t else "buying competes"
    print(f"${home:>9,}  threshold ${t:>7,.0f}  {verdict}")
#> $  300,000  threshold $  1,250  buying competes
#> $  400,000  threshold $  1,667  buying competes
#> $  500,000  threshold $  2,083  rent and invest
#> $  600,000  threshold $  2,500  rent and invest


Edge case: try other unrecoverable rates.


show/hide
print([round(rent_buy_threshold(500000, rate)) for rate in [0.04, 0.05, 0.06]])
#> [1667, 2083, 2500]




Assuming the home value is in A2 and the unrecoverable rate (0.05) is in B2, the threshold goes in C2:
=(A2*B2)/12
With a comparable rent in D2, the verdict goes in E2:
=IF(D2 < C2, "rent and invest", "buying competes")



How to read this result: the threshold is the rent at which renting and owning cost about the same. It’s a quick filter, not a final answer; your plans to stay and your local rents still matter.

title: Major Purchases
text:
3 The Monthly Mortgage Payment
The standard amortization formula spreads the loan plus all future interest into equal monthly payments. Shorter terms mean higher payments but far less total interest.
Formula: M = P × [r(1 + r)^n] ÷ [(1 + r)^n − 1], where P = loan principal, r = annual rate ÷ 12, n = years × 12





Monthly payment on a $480,000 loan at 6% across three terms







Monthly payment on a $480,000 loan at 6% across three terms




Example: a $480,000 loan (a $600,000 home with 20% down) at 6% for 30 years → about $2,878 a month.

RPythonExcel


mortgage_payment() implements the amortization formula.


show/hide
mortgage_payment <- function(principal, annual_rate, years) {
  r <- annual_rate / 12
  n <- years * 12
  principal * (r * (1 + r)^n) / ((1 + r)^n - 1)
}

# $480,000 loan at 6% over 30 years
mortgage_payment(principal = 480000, annual_rate = 0.06, years = 30)
#> [1] 2877.843


The bar chart shows the payment; the total interest is the bigger story. A 15 year loan costs about $1,170 more a month but saves over $300,000 in interest.


show/hide
terms <- data.frame(years = c(15, 20, 30))
terms$payment        <- round(mortgage_payment(480000, 0.06, terms$years))
terms$total_interest <- round(mortgage_payment(480000, 0.06, terms$years) * terms$years * 12 - 480000)
terms
#> # A tibble: 3 × 3
#>   years payment total_interest
#>   <dbl>   <dbl>          <dbl>
#> 1    15    4051         249092
#> 2    20    3439         345329
#> 3    30    2878         556023


Rates matter too. Each point on a 30 year loan moves the payment by roughly $300 a month.


show/hide
round(sapply(c(0.05, 0.06, 0.07), mortgage_payment, principal = 480000, years = 30))
#> [1] 2577 2878 3193


Edge case: at a 0% rate the formula divides zero by zero, so R returns NaN. The payment is then just principal ÷ months.


show/hide
mortgage_payment(480000, 0, 30)
#> [1] NaN
480000 / 360
#> [1] 1333.333




mortgage_payment() implements the amortization formula.


show/hide
def mortgage_payment(principal, annual_rate, years):
    r = annual_rate / 12
    n = years * 12
    return principal * (r * (1 + r) ** n) / ((1 + r) ** n - 1)

# $480,000 loan at 6% over 30 years
print(mortgage_payment(principal=480000, annual_rate=0.06, years=30))
#> 2877.8425207332334


Payment and total interest by term:


show/hide
for years in [15, 20, 30]:
    pmt = mortgage_payment(480000, 0.06, years)
    print(f"{years} yrs  payment ${pmt:,.0f}  total interest ${pmt * years * 12 - 480000:,.0f}")
#> 15 yrs  payment $4,051  total interest $249,092
#> 20 yrs  payment $3,439  total interest $345,329
#> 30 yrs  payment $2,878  total interest $556,023


Payments at three rates on a 30 year loan:


show/hide
print([round(mortgage_payment(480000, rate, 30)) for rate in [0.05, 0.06, 0.07]])
#> [2577, 2878, 3193]


Edge case: at a 0% rate the formula divides by zero (Python raises ZeroDivisionError), so the payment is just principal ÷ months.


show/hide
print(480000 / 360)
#> 1333.3333333333333




Assuming the loan amount is in A2, the annual rate is in B2 (as a decimal), and the years are in C2, the payment goes in D2:
=A2*((B2/12)*(1+B2/12)^(C2*12))/((1+B2/12)^(C2*12)-1)
Excel’s built in PMT() does the same job (flip the sign, since Excel treats the payment as money going out):
=-PMT(B2/12, C2*12, A2)
Total interest goes in E2:
=D2*C2*12-A2

text:
4 Where the First Year’s Payments Go
In month one, interest is the balance times the monthly rate. Only what’s left over reduces the principal.
Formula: First month interest = Principal × (annual rate ÷ 12); First month principal = Monthly payment − First month interest





Interest vs. principal split at three points on a $480,000 / 6% / 30-yr mortgage







Interest vs. principal split at three points on a $480,000 / 6% / 30-yr mortgage




Example: on that $480,000 loan, month one interest is $2,400 of the $2,878 payment, about 83% interest, leaving only about $478 toward principal.

RPythonExcel


first_payment_split() reuses mortgage_payment() from the section above, so it’s repeated here to keep this tab self contained.


show/hide
mortgage_payment <- function(principal, annual_rate, years) {
  r <- annual_rate / 12
  n <- years * 12
  principal * (r * (1 + r)^n) / ((1 + r)^n - 1)
}

first_payment_split <- function(principal, annual_rate, years) {
  payment  <- mortgage_payment(principal, annual_rate, years)
  interest <- principal * (annual_rate / 12)
  data.frame(
    payment      = payment,
    interest     = interest,
    principal    = payment - interest,
    pct_interest = (interest / payment) * 100
  )
}

# first payment on a $480,000 loan at 6% over 30 years
first_payment_split(principal = 480000, annual_rate = 0.06, years = 30)
#> # A tibble: 1 × 4
#>   payment interest principal pct_interest
#>     <dbl>    <dbl>     <dbl>        <dbl>
#> 1   2878.     2400      478.         83.4


One month is a snapshot. Walking the loan month by month and adding up each year shows how slowly the split changes. The first year is about 83% interest, and interest doesn’t drop below half until year 19.


show/hide
amortize <- function(principal, annual_rate, years) {
  r   <- annual_rate / 12
  pmt <- mortgage_payment(principal, annual_rate, years)
  interest <- numeric(years * 12)
  balance  <- principal
  for (m in seq_along(interest)) {
    interest[m] <- balance * r
    balance     <- balance - (pmt - interest[m])
  }
  data.frame(year = rep(seq_len(years), each = 12), interest = interest,
             principal = pmt - interest)
}

sched  <- amortize(480000, 0.06, 30)
by_yr  <- aggregate(cbind(interest, principal) ~ year, data = sched, FUN = sum)
by_yr$pct_interest <- round(by_yr$interest / (by_yr$interest + by_yr$principal) * 100, 1)
by_yr[by_yr$year %in% c(1, 5, 10, 15, 19, 20, 25, 30), ]

def mortgage_payment(principal, annual_rate, years):
    r = annual_rate / 12
    n = years * 12
    return principal * (r * (1 + r) ** n) / ((1 + r) ** n - 1)

def first_payment_split(principal, annual_rate, years):
    payment = mortgage_payment(principal, annual_rate, years)
    interest = principal * (annual_rate / 12)
    return {
        "payment": payment,
        "interest": interest,
        "principal": payment - interest,
        "pct_interest": (interest / payment) * 100,
    }

# first payment on a $480,000 loan at 6% over 30 years

#> {'payment': 2877.8425207332334, 'interest': 2400.0, 'principal': 477.8425207332334, 'pct_interest': 83.39580719616701}


The share of interest by year:


show/hide
def amortize(principal, annual_rate, years):
    r = annual_rate / 12
    pmt = mortgage_payment(principal, annual_rate, years)
    balance, rows = principal, []
    for m in range(years * 12):
        interest = balance * r
        balance -= pmt - interest
        rows.append((m // 12 + 1, interest, pmt - interest))
    return rows

sched = amortize(480000, 0.06, 30)
for year in [1, 5, 10, 15, 19, 20, 25, 30]:
    i = sum(row[1] for row in sched if row[0] == year)
    p = sum(row[2] for row in sched if row[0] == year)
    print(f"year {year:>2}  {i / (i + p):.1%} interest")
#> year  1  82.9% interest
#> year  5  78.3% interest
#> year 10  70.7% interest
#> year 15  60.5% interest
#> year 19  49.9% interest
#> year 20  46.8% interest
#> year 25  28.2% interest
#> year 30  3.2% interest


Principal paid after 5 years:


show/hide
paid_5yr = sum(row[2] for row in sched[:60])
print(f"${paid_5yr:,.0f} paid off, {paid_5yr / 480000:.1%} of the loan")
#> $33,339 paid off, 6.9% of the loan




Assuming the loan amount is in A2, the annual rate is in B2, and the years are in C2, the monthly payment goes in D2:
=-PMT(B2/12, C2*12, A2)
The first month’s interest goes in E2, the principal in F2, and the percent interest in G2 (format as a Percentage):
=A2*B2/12
=D2-E2
=E2/D2
For any year, CUMIPMT() and CUMPRINC() add up the interest and principal between two payment numbers. Year 1 interest, for example:
=-CUMIPMT(B2/12, C2*12, A2, 1, 12, 0)
Principal paid after 5 years:
=-CUMPRINC(B2/12, C2*12, A2, 1, 60, 0)



How to read this result: early on, your payment mostly rents money from the bank. Equity builds slowly at first and quickly at the end, so selling within a few years leaves little principal paid down.

title: Tracking Spending
text:
Tracking vs. budgeting: tracking records where money actually went; budgeting allocates where it should go; comparing the two creates a feedback loop
Capture methods: spending journal, checkbook register, cash envelopes, bank statements; pick one and run it for a full month
Categorizing: start with about 10 stable buckets (housing, transportation, groceries, dining out, subscriptions, personal, health, gifts, fun money, other); when in doubt use “Other”, and only promote a new category after seeing it three months in a row
Using spreadsheets: bank exports have Date, Description, and Amount columns; a keyword lookup adds the Category column in one pass
Monthly review: pull, categorize, compare to budget, and pick one change for next month
Online subscriptions: Americans spend about $219/month on subscriptions and underestimate it by $133; audit every quarter and cancel anything unused in 30 days
Math: the subscription audit, the opportunity cost of a $20/month subscription invested at 7% for 30 years (about $22,700)

text:
5 The Subscription Audit Math
A $20/month subscription feels trivial. Cancel it and invest the $240 a year instead, and the chart below shows what that money grows into at each checkpoint, split into the money you put in and the growth it earned.
Formula: Annual cost × ((1 + r)^n − 1) ÷ r = Opportunity cost in n years
With the book’s 7% real return (the return after inflation), r = 0.07.

section: 2 Your Tax Bill, Bracket by Bracket
text:
2 Your Tax Bill, Bracket by Bracket
Each slice of taxable income is taxed at its own rate. The standard deduction comes off the top first, so those dollars are taxed at 0%.
Formula: Tax = Σ (Rate × Income in that bracket), and Effective rate = Tax ÷ Income





A $45,000 salary, sliced by the standard deduction and 2026 tax brackets







A $45,000 salary, sliced by the standard deduction and 2026 tax brackets




On $45,000, the tax is ($12,400 × 10%) + ($16,500 × 12%) = $3,220. That is an effective rate of about 7.2%, even though the top bracket is 12%.

RPythonExcel




show/hide
income_tax <- function(income, deduction = 16100) {
  taxable <- max(income - deduction, 0)
  lower <- c(0, 12400, 50400, 105700, 201775, 256225, 640600)
  upper <- c(lower[-1], Inf)
  rate  <- c(0.10, 0.12, 0.22, 0.24, 0.32, 0.35, 0.37)
  sum(rate * pmax(pmin(taxable, upper) - lower, 0))
}

marginal_rate <- function(income, deduction = 16100) {
  taxable <- max(income - deduction, 0)
  lower <- c(0, 12400, 50400, 105700, 201775, 256225, 640600)
  rate  <- c(0.10, 0.12, 0.22, 0.24, 0.32, 0.35, 0.37)
  if (taxable == 0) return(0)
  rate[max(which(taxable > lower))]
}

# 2026 federal income tax on a $45,000 salary (single filer)
tax <- income_tax(income = 45000)
tax
#> [1] 3220
tax / 45000
#> [1] 0.07155556

# compare several salaries
salaries <- c(15000, 30000, 45000, 66000, 100000, 150000)
data.frame(
  salary    = salaries,
  tax       = sapply(salaries, income_tax),
  effective = round(sapply(salaries, income_tax) / salaries, 3),
  marginal  = sapply(salaries, marginal_rate)
)
#> # A tibble: 6 × 4
#>   salary   tax effective marginal
#>    <dbl> <dbl>     <dbl>    <dbl>
#> 1  15000     0     0         0   
#> 2  30000  1420     0.047     0.12
#> 3  45000  3220     0.072     0.12
#> 4  66000  5740     0.087     0.12
#> 5 100000 13170     0.132     0.22
#> 6 150000 24734     0.165     0.24


The effective rate is always below the marginal rate. A $15,000 salary owes no federal income tax at all, because it is smaller than the standard deduction.




show/hide
import numpy as np

LOWER = np.array([0, 12400, 50400, 105700, 201775, 256225, 640600])
RATE  = np.array([0.10, 0.12, 0.22, 0.24, 0.32, 0.35, 0.37])

def income_tax(income, deduction=16100):
    taxable = max(income - deduction, 0)
    upper = np.append(LOWER[1:], np.inf)
    return float(np.sum(RATE * np.clip(np.minimum(taxable, upper) - LOWER, 0, None)))

def marginal_rate(income, deduction=16100):
    taxable = max(income - deduction, 0)
    if taxable == 0:
        return 0.0
    return float(RATE[LOWER < taxable][-1])

# 2026 federal income tax on a $45,000 salary (single filer)
tax = income_tax(income=45000)
print(tax)
#> 3220.0
print(round(tax / 45000, 4))
#> 0.0716

# compare several salaries
for s in [15000, 30000, 45000, 66000, 100000, 150000]:
    t = income_tax(s)
    print(f"{s:>7,}  tax ${t:>9,.0f}  effective {t / s:5.1%}  marginal {marginal_rate(s):.0%}")
#>  15,000  tax $        0  effective  0.0%  marginal 0%
#>  30,000  tax $    1,420  effective  4.7%  marginal 12%
#>  45,000  tax $    3,220  effective  7.2%  marginal 12%
#>  66,000  tax $    5,740  effective  8.7%  marginal 12%
#> 100,000  tax $   13,170  effective 13.2%  marginal 22%
#> 150,000  tax $   24,734  effective 16.5%  marginal 24%




Put income in B2. Put the bracket lower limits (0, 12400, 50400, 105700, 201775, 256225, 640600) in E2:E8, the full rates (10%, 12%, 22%, 24%, 32%, 35%, 37%) in F2:F8, and the extra rate each bracket adds over the one below it (10%, 2%, 10%, 2%, 8%, 3%, 2%) in G2:G8.
Tax in C2:
=SUMPRODUCT(--(MAX(B2-16100,0)>E2:E8), MAX(B2-16100,0)-E2:E8, G2:G8)
Effective rate in D2:
=IF(B2>0, C2/B2, 0)
Marginal rate in H2:
=IF(B2<=16100, 0, LOOKUP(MAX(B2-16100,0)-0.01, E2:E8, F2:F8))
Copy row 2 down to compare several salaries.








Marginal rate (steps) vs. effective rate (smooth curve), 2026 single filer







Marginal rate (steps) vs. effective rate (smooth curve), 2026 single filer




How to read this result: the marginal rate tells you what happens to your next dollar. The effective rate tells you what share of your whole salary went to federal income tax. Use the marginal rate for decisions (like a Traditional 401(k) contribution) and the effective rate for budgeting.

title: Taxes
section: 3 How Much of a Raise You Keep
text:
3 How Much of a Raise You Keep
The tax on a raise is the tax on the new income minus the tax on the old income. Only the part of the raise above a bracket line gets the higher rate.
Formula: Tax on raise = Tax(new income) − Tax(old income), and Amount kept = Raise − Tax on raise





A $2,000 raise on a $66,000 salary that crosses into the 22% bracket







A $2,000 raise on a $66,000 salary that crosses into the 22% bracket




On $66,000, taxable income goes from $49,900 to $51,900. The first $500 fills the 12% bracket and the last $1,500 is taxed at 22%. The tax rises from $5,740 to $6,130, so you keep $1,610 of the $2,000 (before FICA and state tax).

RPythonExcel




show/hide
income_tax <- function(income, deduction = 16100) {
  taxable <- max(income - deduction, 0)
  lower <- c(0, 12400, 50400, 105700, 201775, 256225, 640600)
  upper <- c(lower[-1], Inf)
  rate  <- c(0.10, 0.12, 0.22, 0.24, 0.32, 0.35, 0.37)
  sum(rate * pmax(pmin(taxable, upper) - lower, 0))
}

raise_kept <- function(old_income, raise) {
  raise - (income_tax(old_income + raise) - income_tax(old_income))
}

# $2,000 raise on a $66,000 salary
income_tax(66000)
#> [1] 5740
income_tax(68000)
#> [1] 6130
raise_kept(old_income = 66000, raise = 2000)
#> [1] 1610

# the same $2,000 raise at different salaries
old <- c(30000, 45000, 66000, 100000, 150000)
kept <- sapply(old, raise_kept, raise = 2000)
data.frame(old_income = old, kept = kept, share_kept = round(kept / 2000, 3))
#> # A tibble: 5 × 3
#>   old_income  kept share_kept
#>        <dbl> <dbl>      <dbl>
#> 1      30000  1760      0.88 
#> 2      45000  1760      0.88 
#> 3      66000  1610      0.805
#> 4     100000  1560      0.78 
#> 5     150000  1520      0.76

# sanity check: no raise from $1 to $5,000 ever lowers your after tax income
all(sapply(seq(1, 5000, by = 1), raise_kept, old_income = 66000) > 0)
#> [1] TRUE






show/hide
import numpy as np

LOWER = np.array([0, 12400, 50400, 105700, 201775, 256225, 640600])
RATE  = np.array([0.10, 0.12, 0.22, 0.24, 0.32, 0.35, 0.37])

def income_tax(income, deduction=16100):
    taxable = max(income - deduction, 0)
    upper = np.append(LOWER[1:], np.inf)
    return float(np.sum(RATE * np.clip(np.minimum(taxable, upper) - LOWER, 0, None)))

def raise_kept(old_income, raise_amount):
    return raise_amount - (income_tax(old_income + raise_amount) - income_tax(old_income))

# $2,000 raise on a $66,000 salary
print(income_tax(66000), income_tax(68000))
#> 5740.0 6130.0
print(raise_kept(old_income=66000, raise_amount=2000))
#> 1610.0

# the same $2,000 raise at different salaries
for old in [30000, 45000, 66000, 100000, 150000]:
    kept = raise_kept(old, 2000)
    print(f"{old:>7,}  keep ${kept:,.0f} ({kept / 2000:.1%})")
#>  30,000  keep $1,760 (88.0%)
#>  45,000  keep $1,760 (88.0%)
#>  66,000  keep $1,610 (80.5%)
#> 100,000  keep $1,560 (78.0%)
#> 150,000  keep $1,520 (76.0%)

# sanity check: no raise from $1 to $5,000 ever lowers your after tax income
print(all(raise_kept(66000, r) > 0 for r in range(1, 5001)))
#> True




Using the tax formula above, put the old income in B2 and its tax in C2, the new income in B3 and its tax in C3, and the raise in D2.
Amount kept:
=D2-(C3-C2)
Share of the raise kept:
=(D2-(C3-C2))/D2



How to read this result: the share you keep can never drop below 63% (100% minus the top 37% rate). A raise that stays inside one bracket keeps exactly 1 minus that rate. A raise that crosses a line lands somewhere in between.

The examples in this book are written in two free programming languages: R and Python. You don’t need to know either one yet—this page walks you through installing both, no matter which computer you use.






You only have to do this once. Set aside about 20–30 minutes, and feel free to take it one language at a time.



A few words you’ll see along the way:

Install: download a program and add it to your computer, the same way you’d add any app.
Console: a window where you type a command and the computer types back. We use it only to check that things are working.
IDE (Integrated Development Environment): a friendly workspace for writing and running code. Think of it as a word processor built for programming.

3 Number Formatting
Before working through the math, it helps to have two small formatting utilities that handle the $ and % symbols seen throughout the book. They take a plain number and return a reader-friendly string.

RPythonExcel


fmt_dollar() adds a dollar sign, comma separators, and rounds to a set number of decimal places.


show/hide
fmt_dollar <- function(x, digits = 2) {
  paste0("$", formatC(x, format = "f", digits = digits, big.mark = ","))
}


fmt_pct() expects a decimal rate (e.g. 0.07 for 7%) and converts it to a percentage string.


show/hide
fmt_pct <- function(x, digits = 1) {
  paste0(round(x * 100, digits), "%")
}


This can be used to format percentages as strings with a percent sign.


show/hide
fmt_dollar(9200)
#> [1] "$9,200.00"
fmt_dollar(4200.50)
#> [1] "$4,200.50"
fmt_pct(0.07)
#> [1] "7%"
fmt_pct(0.456)
#> [1] "45.6%"




fmt_dollar() uses an f-string with , for thousands and .{digits}f for decimal places.


show/hide
def fmt_dollar(x, digits=2):
    return f"${x:,.{digits}f}"


fmt_pct() takes a decimal rate, multiplies by 100, and formats the result.


show/hide
def fmt_pct(x, digits=1):
    return f"{x * 100:.{digits}f}%"


Utility functions like fmt_pct() can be re-used in other, more complex functions.


show/hide
print(fmt_dollar(9200))
#> $9,200.00
print(fmt_dollar(4200.50))
#> $4,200.50
print(fmt_pct(0.07))
#> 7.0%
print(fmt_pct(0.456))
#> 45.6%




In Excel, number formatting is applied through the toolbar. Select the cells to format and choose the appropriate option from the Number Format dropdown.







Common number formats in Excel


There are two options for money: Currency and Accounting.1



Both fmt_dollar() and fmt_pct() follow the same convention: input is always a plain number, output is always a string. They are used throughout the remaining sections to clean up results.

title: Income
text:
4 The Wealth Formula
Galloway’s formula becomes real numbers when we picture someone earning $62,400 a year (about the 2025 median for full time workers). They save 15% ($9,360) every year and earn 8%. Each bar below is their savings at a checkpoint, split into what they put in and what it grew into.
Formula: Wealth after n years = Yearly savings × [((1 + r)^n − 1) ÷ r]
Yearly savings = Income × Savings rate, r is the yearly return, and n is the number of years.





$9,360 saved every year at 8%: money put in vs. growth







$9,360 saved every year at 8%: money put in vs. growth




The blue layer grows in a straight line, one $9,360 deposit per year. The green layer is growth, and it passes the blue layer after about year 18.

RPythonExcel


wealth_formula() returns the future value of saving a fixed amount every year.


show/hide
wealth_formula <- function(median_income, savings_rate, annual_return, years) {
  # future value of saving a fixed amount every year (contributions plus growth)
  annual_savings <- median_income * savings_rate
  annual_savings * (((1 + annual_return)^years - 1) / annual_return)
}


After 40 years with median income, a 15% savings rate, and an 8% return:


show/hide
wealth_formula(
  median_income = 62400,
  savings_rate = 0.15,
  annual_return = 0.08,
  years = 40
) |> fmt_dollar()
#> [1] "$2,424,769.02"


The function is vectorized, so we can pass several checkpoints at once and split each total into money put in and growth:


show/hide
yrs <- c(10, 18, 20, 30, 40)
total <- wealth_formula(62400, 0.15, 0.08, yrs)
put_in <- 62400 * 0.15 * yrs
data.frame(
  years  = yrs,
  put_in = fmt_dollar(put_in, 0),
  growth = fmt_dollar(total - put_in, 0),
  total  = fmt_dollar(total, 0)
)
#> # A tibble: 5 × 4
#>   years put_in   growth     total     
#>   <dbl> <chr>    <chr>      <chr>     
#> 1    10 $93,600  $41,994    $135,594  
#> 2    18 $168,480 $182,054   $350,534  
#> 3    20 $187,200 $241,132   $428,332  
#> 4    30 $280,800 $779,531   $1,060,331
#> 5    40 $374,400 $2,050,369 $2,424,769


Year 18 is the first checkpoint where growth is bigger than the money put in.
Stoicism is the savings rate. Here is the same income at three savings rates after 40 years:


show/hide
rates <- c(0.10, 0.15, 0.20)
data.frame(
  savings_rate = fmt_pct(rates),
  yearly       = fmt_dollar(62400 * rates, 0),
  after_40     = fmt_dollar(wealth_formula(62400, rates, 0.08, 40), 0)
)
#> # A tibble: 3 × 3
#>   savings_rate yearly  after_40  
#>   <chr>        <chr>   <chr>     
#> 1 10%          $6,240  $1,616,513
#> 2 15%          $9,360  $2,424,769
#> 3 20%          $12,480 $3,233,025


Two edge cases are worth checking. A savings rate of zero collapses the whole term to zero, just like Galloway’s formula says. A return of exactly zero divides by zero, so R returns NaN; with no growth the answer is simply yearly savings × years.


show/hide
wealth_formula(62400, savings_rate = 0, annual_return = 0.08, years = 40)
#> [1] 0
wealth_formula(62400, savings_rate = 0.15, annual_return = 0, years = 40)
#> [1] NaN
62400 * 0.15 * 40
#> [1] 374400


How to read this result: about $2.4 million after 40 years, and only $374,400 of it is money you put in. Time and growth did the rest.


The Python version of wealth_formula() works the same way:


show/hide
def wealth_formula(median_income, savings_rate, annual_return, years):
    # future value of saving a fixed amount every year (contributions plus growth)
    annual_savings = median_income * savings_rate
    return annual_savings * (((1 + annual_return)**years - 1) / annual_return)


After 40 years with median income, a 15% savings rate, and an 8% return:


show/hide
fmt_dollar(wealth_formula(
    median_income=62400,
    savings_rate=0.15,
    annual_return=0.08,
    years=40
))
#> '$2,424,769.02'


Plain Python numbers are not vectorized, so we loop over the checkpoints:


show/hide
for yrs in [10, 18, 20, 30, 40]:
    total = wealth_formula(62400, 0.15, 0.08, yrs)
    put_in = 62400 * 0.15 * yrs
    print(f"{yrs:>3} yrs  put in {fmt_dollar(put_in, 0):>10}  "
          f"growth {fmt_dollar(total - put_in, 0):>11}  total {fmt_dollar(total, 0):>11}")
#>  10 yrs  put in    $93,600  growth     $41,994  total    $135,594
#>  18 yrs  put in   $168,480  growth    $182,054  total    $350,534
#>  20 yrs  put in   $187,200  growth    $241,132  total    $428,332
#>  30 yrs  put in   $280,800  growth    $779,531  total  $1,060,331
#>  40 yrs  put in   $374,400  growth  $2,050,369  total  $2,424,769


The same income at three savings rates after 40 years:


show/hide
for rate in [0.10, 0.15, 0.20]:
    print(f"{fmt_pct(rate):>6}  {fmt_dollar(62400 * rate, 0):>8}/yr  "
          f"{fmt_dollar(wealth_formula(62400, rate, 0.08, 40), 0):>12}")
#>  10.0%    $6,240/yr    $1,616,513
#>  15.0%    $9,360/yr    $2,424,769
#>  20.0%   $12,480/yr    $3,233,025


A savings rate of zero returns zero. A return of exactly zero raises a ZeroDivisionError in Python (R returns NaN instead), so with no growth use yearly savings × years:


show/hide
print(wealth_formula(62400, savings_rate=0, annual_return=0.08, years=40))
#> 0.0
try:
    wealth_formula(62400, savings_rate=0.15, annual_return=0, years=40)
except ZeroDivisionError:
    print("No growth:", fmt_dollar(62400 * 0.15 * 40))
#> No growth: $374,400.00




Put the inputs in one row:

A2: median income (62400)
B2: savings rate (0.15)
C2: annual return (0.08)
D2: years (40)

Total contributed (the money put in) in E2:
=A2*B2*D2
Total wealth, contributions plus growth, in F2:
=(A2*B2)*(((1+C2)^D2-1)/C2)
Excel’s built in FV() gives the same $2,424,769 (enter the yearly savings as a negative number because it is cash leaving your pocket):
=FV(C2, D2, -A2*B2)
Growth alone in G2:
=F2-E2
F2 already includes everything in E2, so don’t add the two together. To compare savings rates, fill B3:B4 with 0.10 and 0.20 and copy the row down.

text:
5 Fixed-Cost Ratio
Fixed costs (rent, loan payments, insurance, utilities) are the bills you can’t easily change month to month. Picture a first job with $3,200 of take-home pay a month and $1,760 of fixed costs. The bar below cuts that paycheck into 10 equal pieces of $320 (each piece is 10%).
Formula: Fixed-Cost Ratio = Fixed Costs ÷ Take-Home Pay × 100





$3,200 take-home pay in 10 units of $320: fixed costs vs. flexible spending







$3,200 take-home pay in 10 units of $320: fixed costs vs. flexible spending




The red section covers 5 and a half of the 10 pieces, so fixed costs take 55% of the paycheck. The ceiling is 60% of $3,200, or $1,920.

RPythonExcel




show/hide
fixed_cost_ratio <- function(fixed_costs, take_home) {
  (fixed_costs / take_home) * 100
}


$1,760 of fixed costs on $3,200 take-home pay:


show/hide
fixed_cost_ratio(fixed_costs = 1760, take_home = 3200)
#> [1] 55


How much room is left under the 60% ceiling?


show/hide
ceiling_60 <- 3200 * 0.60
ceiling_60
#> [1] 1920
ceiling_60 - 1760
#> [1] 160


The ratio works on several budgets at once. Below, the same $1,760 of fixed costs is compared against three paychecks, plus a higher rent on the original paycheck:


show/hide
budgets <- data.frame(
  scenario    = c("First job", "Lower pay", "After a raise", "Pricier apartment"),
  fixed_costs = c(1760, 1760, 1760, 2160),
  take_home   = c(3200, 2800, 3600, 3200)
)
budgets$ratio    <- round(fixed_cost_ratio(budgets$fixed_costs, budgets$take_home), 1)
budgets$under_60 <- budgets$ratio <= 60
budgets
#> # A tibble: 4 × 5
#>   scenario    fixed_costs take_home ratio under_60
#>   <chr>             <dbl>     <dbl> <dbl> <lgl>   
#> 1 First job          1760      3200  55   TRUE    
#> 2 Lower pay          1760      2800  62.9 FALSE   
#> 3 After a ra…        1760      3600  48.9 TRUE    
#> 4 Pricier ap…        2160      3200  67.5 FALSE


How to read this result: anything at or under 60 leaves at least 40% of the paycheck for savings and flexible spending. A $400 jump in rent pushes the same paycheck to 67.5%, over the line.




show/hide
def fixed_cost_ratio(fixed_costs, take_home):
    return (fixed_costs / take_home) * 100


$1,760 of fixed costs on $3,200 take-home pay:


show/hide
fixed_cost_ratio(fixed_costs=1760, take_home=3200)
#> 55.00000000000001


Python prints 55.00000000000001 because computers store decimals in binary, which adds a tiny rounding error. Wrap the result in round() for display:


show/hide
round(fixed_cost_ratio(fixed_costs=1760, take_home=3200), 1)
#> 55.0


Room left under the 60% ceiling:


show/hide
ceiling_60 = 3200 * 0.60
print(fmt_dollar(ceiling_60), fmt_dollar(ceiling_60 - 1760))
#> $1,920.00 $160.00


The same comparison across four budgets:


show/hide
budgets = [
    ("First job", 1760, 3200),
    ("Lower pay", 1760, 2800),
    ("After a raise", 1760, 3600),
    ("Pricier apartment", 2160, 3200),
]
for scenario, fixed, pay in budgets:
    ratio = fixed_cost_ratio(fixed, pay)
    print(f"{scenario:<18} {ratio:5.1f}  under 60: {ratio <= 60}")
#> First job           55.0  under 60: True
#> Lower pay           62.9  under 60: False
#> After a raise       48.9  under 60: True
#> Pricier apartment   67.5  under 60: False




Enter fixed costs in A2 (1760) and take-home pay in B2 (3200), then in C2:
=A2/B2*100
That gives 55. Or enter =A2/B2 and format C2 as a percentage (Home → %) to display 55%. For a percent string:
=TEXT(A2/B2, "0.0%")

The room left under the 60% ceiling, in D2:
=B2*0.6-A2
A pass/fail flag in E2:
=IF(A2/B2<=0.6, "Under 60%", "Over 60%")
Add more budgets in rows 3 to 5 and fill C2:E2 down.

title: Income
text:
6 Using Pipes in R
The pipe operator (|>) passes the output of one function directly into the next function as its first argument, so the code reads left to right instead of inside out. fixed_cost_ratio() already multiplies by 100, so we can pipe its result into round() and then paste0() to add the percent sign.
fixed_cost_ratio(fixed_costs = 1760, take_home = 3200) |> round(1) |> paste0("%")
Read that as: compute the ratio, then round it, then add the %. The version without a pipe nests the calls and reads from the inside out, which is harder to follow.
paste0(round(fixed_cost_ratio(fixed_costs = 1760, take_home = 3200), 1), "%")
When steps always belong together, wrap them in a single function so callers only see one name.

fixed_cost_pct <- function(fixed_costs, take_home) {
  fixed_cost_ratio(fixed_costs, take_home) |>
    round(1) |>
    paste0("%")
}


fixed_cost_pct(fixed_costs = 1760, take_home = 3200)
#> [1] "55%"

Python has no native pipe operator. The equivalent is storing the result from fixed_cost_ratio() in a variable and passing it to the next step:

def fixed_cost_pct(fixed_costs, take_home):
    ratio = fixed_cost_ratio(fixed_costs, take_home)
    return f"{ratio:.1f}%"


fixed_cost_pct(fixed_costs=1760, take_home=3200)
#> '55.0%'

Python’s approach emphasizes explicit intermediate steps. This reads top to bottom and makes debugging easier since you can inspect ratio along the way.
Read more about the pipe operator in R vs. Python.

section: 7 What a Raise Is Really Worth
text:
7 What a Raise Is Really Worth
Say a raise adds $400 a month to your take-home pay, and you split it: $200 goes to your lifestyle and $200 gets invested. The chart shows what that single habit produces at 7% over 25 years.
Formula: FV = PMT × [((1 + r)^n − 1) ÷ r]
PMT is the amount invested each month, r is the monthly return (7% ÷ 12), and n is the number of months (25 × 12 = 300).





$200/month invested at 7%: value at each 5-year checkpoint







$200/month invested at 7%: value at each 5-year checkpoint





RPythonExcel




show/hide
raise_invested_value <- function(monthly_raise, invest_share, rate, years) {
  contribution <- monthly_raise * invest_share
  monthly_rate <- rate / 12
  periods      <- years * 12
  contribution * (((1 + monthly_rate)^periods - 1) / monthly_rate)
}


Half of a $400/month raise, invested for 25 years at 7%:


show/hide
raise_invested_value(
  monthly_raise = 400,
  invest_share = 0.5,
  rate = 0.07,
  years = 25) |> fmt_dollar()
#> [1] "$162,014.34"


Sanity check: you put in $200 × 300 months = $60,000, so growth added about $102,000.


show/hide
fv <- raise_invested_value(400, 0.5, 0.07, 25)
put_in <- 200 * 25 * 12
c(put_in = put_in, growth = round(fv - put_in))
#> put_in growth 
#>  60000 102014


How big a share should you invest? Here is the same $400 raise split four ways, over 25 years:


show/hide
shares <- c(0.25, 0.50, 0.75, 1.00)
data.frame(
  invest_share = fmt_pct(shares, 0),
  monthly      = fmt_dollar(400 * shares, 0),
  after_25     = fmt_dollar(raise_invested_value(400, shares, 0.07, 25), 0)
)
#> # A tibble: 4 × 3
#>   invest_share monthly after_25
#>   <chr>        <chr>   <chr>   
#> 1 25%          $100    $81,007 
#> 2 50%          $200    $162,014
#> 3 75%          $300    $243,022
#> 4 100%         $400    $324,029


How to read this result: every extra $100 a month you invest adds about $81,000 after 25 years. Even the 25% split grows to more than $80,000.




show/hide
def raise_invested_value(monthly_raise, invest_share, rate, years):
    contribution = monthly_raise * invest_share
    monthly_rate = rate / 12
    periods = years * 12
    return contribution * (((1 + monthly_rate) ** periods - 1) / monthly_rate)


Half of a $400/month raise, invested for 25 years at 7%:


show/hide
fmt_dollar(raise_invested_value(monthly_raise=400, invest_share=0.5, rate=0.07, years=25))
#> '$162,014.34'


Sanity check on money put in vs. growth:


show/hide
fv = raise_invested_value(400, 0.5, 0.07, 25)
put_in = 200 * 25 * 12
print(fmt_dollar(put_in, 0), fmt_dollar(fv - put_in, 0))
#> $60,000 $102,014


The same $400 raise split four ways:


show/hide
for share in [0.25, 0.50, 0.75, 1.00]:
    print(f"{fmt_pct(share, 0):>5}  {fmt_dollar(400 * share, 0):>5}/mo  "
          f"{fmt_dollar(raise_invested_value(400, share, 0.07, 25), 0):>9}")
#>   25%   $100/mo    $81,007
#>   50%   $200/mo   $162,014
#>   75%   $300/mo   $243,022
#>  100%   $400/mo   $324,029




Use the built in FV() function: FV(rate, nper, pmt).

rate: monthly return = 7%/12
nper: number of months = 25*12
pmt: monthly contribution as a negative = -200

=FV(7%/12, 25*12, -200)





This returns $162,014.34. To compare splits, put the raise in A2 (400), the share in B2 (0.5), the yearly rate in C2 (0.07), and the years in D2 (25), then in E2:
=FV(C2/12, D2*12, -A2*B2)
Fill rows 3 to 5 with shares of 0.25, 0.75, and 1, and copy E2 down. Money put in, in F2:
=A2*B2*D2*12

What a retirement account is: a container, not an investment; it decides how the investments inside get taxed; early withdrawals before 59 and a half usually cost a 10% penalty plus income tax
2026 limits: 401(k)/403(b)/TSP $24,500; Traditional and Roth IRA $7,500 (one shared limit); HSA $4,400 (self); taxable brokerage has no limit

text:
2 The Employer Match
Your employer adds money on top of what you put in, up to a limit.
Formula: Match = Salary × min(Your %, Match limit %) × Match rate
Example: $45,000 × min(6%, 6%) × 50% = $1,350 a year in free money. At 3%, you’d only get $675.





6% of a $45,000 salary, plus a 50% employer match







6% of a $45,000 salary, plus a 50% employer match




The second example runs the same job across several contribution rates. Past 6%, your own deposits keep growing but the match stops. The last example shows what one year of the full match becomes if it stays invested for 40 years at 7%.

RPythonExcel




show/hide
employer_match <- function(salary, contribution_pct, match_limit_pct, match_rate) {
  salary * pmin(contribution_pct, match_limit_pct) * match_rate
}

# $45,000 salary, 6% contribution, 50% match on the first 6%
employer_match(salary = 45000, contribution_pct = 0.06,
               match_limit_pct = 0.06, match_rate = 0.50)
#> [1] 1350

# same job, but only contributing 3%
employer_match(salary = 45000, contribution_pct = 0.03,
               match_limit_pct = 0.06, match_rate = 0.50)
#> [1] 675

# several contribution rates
pct <- c(0, 0.03, 0.06, 0.10, 0.15)
data.frame(
  your_pct     = pct * 100,
  you_put_in   = 45000 * pct,
  match        = employer_match(45000, pct, 0.06, 0.50),
  match_missed = 1350 - employer_match(45000, pct, 0.06, 0.50)
)
#> # A tibble: 5 × 4
#>   your_pct you_put_in match match_missed
#>      <dbl>      <dbl> <dbl>        <dbl>
#> 1        0          0     0         1350
#> 2        3       1350   675          675
#> 3        6       2700  1350            0
#> 4       10       4500  1350            0
#> 5       15       6750  1350            0

# one year of the full match, invested for 40 years at 7%
1350 * 1.07^40
#> [1] 20215.52






show/hide
def employer_match(salary, contribution_pct, match_limit_pct, match_rate):
    return salary * min(contribution_pct, match_limit_pct) * match_rate

# $45,000 salary, 6% contribution, 50% match on the first 6%
print(employer_match(salary=45000, contribution_pct=0.06,
                     match_limit_pct=0.06, match_rate=0.50))
#> 1350.0

# same job, but only contributing 3%
print(employer_match(salary=45000, contribution_pct=0.03,
                     match_limit_pct=0.06, match_rate=0.50))
#> 675.0

# several contribution rates
for pct in [0, 0.03, 0.06, 0.10, 0.15]:
    m = employer_match(45000, pct, 0.06, 0.50)
    print(f"{pct:>4.0%}: you ${45000 * pct:>6,.0f}, match ${m:>5,.0f}, missed ${1350 - m:>5,.0f}")
#>   0%: you $     0, match $    0, missed $1,350
#>   3%: you $ 1,350, match $  675, missed $  675
#>   6%: you $ 2,700, match $1,350, missed $    0
#>  10%: you $ 4,500, match $1,350, missed $    0
#>  15%: you $ 6,750, match $1,350, missed $    0

# one year of the full match, invested for 40 years at 7%
print(1350 * 1.07 ** 40)
#> 20215.51808292943




With Salary in B2, Your % in C2, Match limit % in D2, and Match rate in E2:
=B2 * MIN(C2, D2) * E2
List several rates down column C and copy the formula down to see where the match stops growing.



Read the match as a 50% return the day you deposit. Contributing 3% instead of 6% leaves $675 a year on the table, and one year of the full match grows to about $20,200 over 40 years at 7%.

title: Retirement Accounts
text:
3 Traditional vs. Roth
Roth takes the tax out first, then the rest grows. Traditional lets the whole amount grow, then takes the tax out at the end.
Formula: Amount you keep = Contribution × (1 − tax rate) × (1 + r)^n
For Roth, use today’s tax rate. For Traditional, use your tax rate in retirement.
Example: $1,000 for 40 years at 7%. With 12% now and 12% later, both accounts leave you about $13,178. If your rate in retirement is 22% instead, the Traditional account leaves you about $11,680.





$1,000 after 40 years at 7%, with a 12% tax rate now and later







$1,000 after 40 years at 7%, with a 12% tax rate now and later




Multiplying by (1 − tax rate) gives the same answer whether you do it first or last. So the second example holds today’s rate at 12% and tries several retirement rates. The edge case is a retirement rate lower than today’s, where Traditional wins.

RPythonExcel




show/hide
after_tax_value <- function(contribution, tax_rate, rate, years) {
  contribution * (1 - tax_rate) * (1 + rate)^years
}

# Roth: taxed at today's 12% rate
after_tax_value(contribution = 1000, tax_rate = 0.12, rate = 0.07, years = 40)
#> [1] 13177.52

# Traditional: taxed at a 22% rate in retirement
after_tax_value(contribution = 1000, tax_rate = 0.22, rate = 0.07, years = 40)
#> [1] 11680.08

# sanity check: same rate now and later gives the same answer
all.equal(1000 * (1 - 0.12) * 1.07^40, 1000 * 1.07^40 * (1 - 0.12))
#> [1] TRUE

# today's rate is 12%; try several retirement rates
later <- c(0.10, 0.12, 0.22, 0.24)
roth  <- after_tax_value(1000, 0.12, 0.07, 40)
trad  <- after_tax_value(1000, later, 0.07, 40)
data.frame(
  retirement_rate = later * 100,
  roth            = round(roth),
  traditional     = round(trad),
  winner          = ifelse(abs(roth - trad) < 1, "tie",
                           ifelse(roth > trad, "Roth", "Traditional"))
)
#> # A tibble: 4 × 4
#>   retirement_rate  roth traditional winner     
#>             <dbl> <dbl>       <dbl> <chr>      
#> 1              10 13178       13477 Traditional
#> 2              12 13178       13178 tie        
#> 3              22 13178       11680 Roth       
#> 4              24 13178       11381 Roth

def after_tax_value(contribution, tax_rate, rate, years):
    return contribution * (1 - tax_rate) * (1 + rate) ** years

# Roth: taxed at today's 12% rate
print(after_tax_value(contribution=1000, tax_rate=0.12, rate=0.07, years=40))
#> 13177.522898502146

# Traditional: taxed at a 22% rate in retirement
print(after_tax_value(contribution=1000, tax_rate=0.22, rate=0.07, years=40))
#> 11680.077114581447

roth = after_tax_value(1000, 0.12, 0.07, 40)
for later in [0.10, 0.12, 0.22, 0.24]:
    trad = after_tax_value(1000, later, 0.07, 40)
    winner = "tie" if abs(roth - trad) < 1 else ("Roth" if roth > trad else "Traditional")

With Contribution in B2, Tax rate in C2, Return in D2, and Years in E2:
=B2 * (1 - C2) * (1 + D2) ^ E2
Put today’s rate in one row and the retirement rate in the next; the row with the larger result wins.



Read the result as a contest between two tax rates. Growth and years don’t pick the winner. Roth wins when today’s rate is lower than your rate in retirement, and Traditional wins when it’s higher.

title: Retirement Accounts
text:
4 Cashing Out vs. Rolling Over
The book’s job change example: cash out $5,000 at 22, or leave it invested until 67.
Formula: Cash in hand = Balance × (1 − tax rate − penalty); Left invested = Balance × (1 + r)^n
Example: $5,000 × (1 − 0.12 − 0.10) = $3,900 today, vs. $5,000 × 1.07^45 ≈ $105,000 at 67 (the book rounds to about $100,000).

RPythonExcel




show/hide
cash_out <- function(balance, tax_rate, penalty = 0.10) {
  balance * (1 - tax_rate - penalty)
}

cash_out(balance = 5000, tax_rate = 0.12)
#> [1] 3900
5000 * 1.07^(67 - 22)
#> [1] 105012.3

# several balances
bal <- c(2000, 5000, 20000)
data.frame(balance = bal, cash_now = cash_out(bal, 0.12), at_67 = round(bal * 1.07^45))
#> # A tibble: 3 × 3
#>   balance cash_now  at_67
#>     <dbl>    <dbl>  <dbl>
#> 1    2000     1560  42005
#> 2    5000     3900 105012
#> 3   20000    15600 420049






show/hide
def cash_out(balance, tax_rate, penalty=0.10):
    return balance * (1 - tax_rate - penalty)

print(cash_out(balance=5000, tax_rate=0.12))
#> 3900.0
print(5000 * 1.07 ** (67 - 22))
#> 105012.2587933697

for bal in [2000, 5000, 20000]:
    print(f"${bal:,}: cash now ${cash_out(bal, 0.12):,.0f}, at 67 ${bal * 1.07 ** 45:,.0f}")

Read it as a trade: $3,900 now costs you about $100,000 later.

title: Savings Strategies
text:
2 Savings Rate
The savings rate is the slice of your income bar that goes to savings. Every dollar goes to either spending or savings, so the rate measures how big the savings slice is.
Formula: Savings Rate = (Income − Spending) ÷ Income × 100
Example: you take home $5,000 and spend $3,500. (5,000 − 3,500) ÷ 5,000 = 30% savings rate.





Savings slice as a percentage of income (same $60k income, different rates)







Savings slice as a percentage of income (same $60k income, different rates)





RPythonExcel


savings_rate() subtracts spending from income and divides by income.


show/hide
savings_rate <- function(income, spending) {
  ((income - spending) / income) * 100
}

# $5,000 take-home, $3,500 spent
savings_rate(income = 5000, spending = 3500)
#> [1] 30


The function is vectorized, so we can check several spending levels at once and label each with its benchmark tier. The last row spends more than it earns, which gives a negative rate.


show/hide
spending <- c(4700, 4250, 3750, 3250, 5200)
rates <- savings_rate(income = 5000, spending = spending)
data.frame(
  spending = spending,
  rate     = round(rates, 1),
  tier     = cut(rates,
                 breaks = c(-Inf, 10, 20, 30, Inf),
                 labels = c("Danger zone", "Average", "Strong", "FI path"),
                 right  = FALSE)
)
#> # A tibble: 5 × 3
#>   spending  rate tier       
#>      <dbl> <dbl> <fct>      
#> 1     4700     6 Danger zone
#> 2     4250    15 Average    
#> 3     3750    25 Strong     
#> 4     3250    35 FI path    
#> 5     5200    -4 Danger zone


Flip the formula to find the spending limit for a target rate: Spending = Income × (1 − Rate). Plugging it back in should return the rate we started with.


show/hide
spending_limit <- function(income, target_rate) {
  income * (1 - target_rate)
}
spending_limit(income = 5000, target_rate = 0.30)
#> [1] 3500
savings_rate(income = 5000, spending = spending_limit(5000, 0.30))
#> [1] 30




The Python version of savings_rate() works the same way.


show/hide
def savings_rate(income, spending):
    return ((income - spending) / income) * 100

# $5,000 take-home, $3,500 spent
savings_rate(income=5000, spending=3500)
#> 30.0


Check several spending levels and label each with its benchmark tier. A negative rate means spending is higher than income.


show/hide
def rate_tier(rate):
    if rate < 10:
        return "Danger zone"
    elif rate < 20:
        return "Average"
    elif rate < 30:
        return "Strong"
    return "FI path"

for spending in [4700, 4250, 3750, 3250, 5200]:
    rate = savings_rate(income=5000, spending=spending)
    print(f"${spending:>6,}  {rate:6.1f}%  {rate_tier(rate)}")
#> $ 4,700     6.0%  Danger zone
#> $ 4,250    15.0%  Average
#> $ 3,750    25.0%  Strong
#> $ 3,250    35.0%  FI path
#> $ 5,200    -4.0%  Danger zone


Flip the formula to find the spending limit for a target rate, then plug it back in as a check.


show/hide
def spending_limit(income, target_rate):
    return income * (1 - target_rate)

limit = spending_limit(income=5000, target_rate=0.30)
print(limit)
#> 3500.0
print(savings_rate(income=5000, spending=limit))
#> 30.0




Assuming Income is in cell B2 and Spending is in cell C2, the savings rate goes in D2:
=((B2 - C2) / B2) * 100
To label the benchmark tier in E2:
=IFS(D2 < 10, "Danger zone", D2 < 20, "Average", D2 < 30, "Strong", TRUE, "FI path")
To find the spending limit for a target rate (as a decimal) in F2:
=B2 * (1 - F2)



How to read this result: a 30% rate means 30 cents of every dollar you bring home stays with you. If the rate is negative, you are spending more than you earn and the gap is coming from savings or debt.

title: Savings Strategies
text:
3 Years to a Savings Target
The book compares two savers at a 7% return. One earns $40,000 and saves 40% ($16,000 a year). The other earns $120,000 and saves 10% ($12,000 a year). The bigger saver reaches $500,000 first. We can solve for the number of years directly.
Formula: Years = ln(1 + Target × r ÷ Annual Savings) ÷ ln(1 + r)
Example: ln(1 + 500,000 × 0.07 ÷ 16,000) ÷ ln(1.07) = 17.1 years, so the balance passes $500k during year 18. At $12,000 a year it takes 20.2 years, so year 21.





Years to reach $500,000 at a 7% return on a $60,000 income







Years to reach $500,000 at a 7% return on a $60,000 income





RPythonExcel


years_to_target() solves the savings growth formula for time. ceiling() gives the year the balance actually passes the target.


show/hide
years_to_target <- function(annual_savings, target, rate = 0.07) {
  log(1 + target * rate / annual_savings) / log(1 + rate)
}

# $40k at 40% vs. $120k at 10%
yrs <- years_to_target(annual_savings = c(16000, 12000), target = 500000)
round(yrs, 1)
#> [1] 17.1 20.2
ceiling(yrs)
#> [1] 18 21


Same $60,000 income, four savings rates. Saving nothing never gets there, so the last row returns Inf.


show/hide
rate <- c(0.08, 0.15, 0.25, 0.35, 0)
data.frame(
  rate   = rate,
  saved  = 60000 * rate,
  years  = round(years_to_target(60000 * rate, target = 500000), 1)
)
#> # A tibble: 5 × 3
#>    rate saved years
#>   <dbl> <dbl> <dbl>
#> 1  0.08  4800  31.3
#> 2  0.15  9000  23.5
#> 3  0.25 15000  17.8
#> 4  0.35 21000  14.5
#> 5  0        0 Inf


Sanity check: grow $16,000 a year for 17 and 18 years. The balance should be just under $500k after 17 and over it after 18.


show/hide
fv_annual <- function(annual_savings, years, rate = 0.07) {
  annual_savings * ((1 + rate)^years - 1) / rate
}
round(fv_annual(16000, years = c(17, 18)))
#> [1] 493443 543985




years_to_target() solves the savings growth formula for time. math.ceil() gives the year the balance passes the target.


show/hide
import math

def years_to_target(annual_savings, target, rate=0.07):
    if annual_savings <= 0:
        return math.inf
    return math.log(1 + target * rate / annual_savings) / math.log(1 + rate)

# $40k at 40% vs. $120k at 10%
for saved in [16000, 12000]:
    yrs = years_to_target(annual_savings=saved, target=500000)
    print(f"${saved:,}/yr: {yrs:.1f} years (passes target in year {math.ceil(yrs)})")
#> $16,000/yr: 17.1 years (passes target in year 18)
#> $12,000/yr: 20.2 years (passes target in year 21)


Same $60,000 income, four savings rates. Saving nothing never reaches the target.


show/hide
for rate in [0.08, 0.15, 0.25, 0.35, 0]:
    saved = 60000 * rate
    print(f"{rate:4.0%}  ${saved:>7,.0f}/yr  {years_to_target(saved, 500000):5.1f} years")
#>   8%  $  4,800/yr   31.3 years
#>  15%  $  9,000/yr   23.5 years
#>  25%  $ 15,000/yr   17.8 years
#>  35%  $ 21,000/yr   14.5 years
#>   0%  $      0/yr    inf years


Sanity check: the balance should be just under $500k after 17 years and over it after 18.


show/hide
def fv_annual(annual_savings, years, rate=0.07):
    return annual_savings * ((1 + rate) ** years - 1) / rate

[round(fv_annual(16000, years)) for years in [17, 18]]
#> [493443, 543985]




Assuming Annual_Savings is in cell B2, the return Rate is in C2, and the Target is in D2:
=LN(1 + D2 * C2 / B2) / LN(1 + C2)
Excel’s NPER() gives the same answer (savings entered as a negative cash flow):
=NPER(C2, -B2, 0, D2)
Wrap either one in ROUNDUP(..., 0) to get the year the balance passes the target.



How to read this result: the answer is the number of years of steady saving needed, not counting anything you already have. Raising the savings rate shortens the timeline much more at low rates than at high ones.

title: Insurance
text:
The rule: insure losses you can’t absorb; cover small ones from your emergency fund (leave room for error)
Insurance words: premium, deductible, claim, coverage limit, liability; premiums and deductibles move in opposite directions
Health insurance: never go without; stay on a parent’s plan until 26, get it through work, or use the marketplace; copay, coinsurance, and the out of pocket maximum (your worst case, capped at $10,600 in 2026); high deductible plans qualify for an HSA with a deductible of at least $1,700 and an out of pocket maximum of no more than $8,500
Auto insurance: liability of at least 100/300/100; consider dropping collision and comprehensive on a cheap car
Renters insurance: about $13 to $23 a month; choose replacement cost over actual cash value
Disability insurance: about 1 in 4 of today’s 20 year olds will become disabled before retirement age; take employer long term disability (about 60% of pay)
Life insurance: only if someone depends on your income; buy term, about 10 times yearly income; skip whole life
Umbrella insurance: $1 million or more of extra liability; revisit as net worth grows
What to skip: extended warranties, phone insurance, life insurance with no dependents, single event policies

text:
2 Choosing a Deductible
A higher deductible lowers your premium but costs more on each claim. The break even point is how many years of premium savings it takes to cover the extra deductible.
Formula: Break even years = (Higher deductible − Lower deductible) ÷ Yearly premium savings





Savings from a $1,000 deductible vs. a $500 deductible, year by year







Savings from a $1,000 deductible vs. a $500 deductible, year by year




Car insurance costs $1,500 a year with a $500 deductible, or $1,350 with a $1,000 deductible. ($1,000 − $500) ÷ $150 = about 3.3 years. If you file a claim less often than that, the higher deductible comes out ahead.

RPythonExcel




show/hide
break_even_years <- function(high_deductible, low_deductible, yearly_savings) {
  (high_deductible - low_deductible) / yearly_savings
}

# $1,000 vs. $500 deductible, saving $150 a year
break_even_years(high_deductible = 1000, low_deductible = 500, yearly_savings = 150)
#> [1] 3.333333

# other quotes you might see
quotes <- data.frame(
  high    = c(1000, 1000, 1000, 2000, 2000),
  low     = c(500, 500, 500, 500, 1000),
  savings = c(50, 150, 300, 250, 120)
)
quotes$break_even <- round(break_even_years(quotes$high, quotes$low, quotes$savings), 1)
quotes
#> # A tibble: 5 × 4
#>    high   low savings break_even
#>   <dbl> <dbl>   <dbl>      <dbl>
#> 1  1000   500      50       10  
#> 2  1000   500     150        3.3
#> 3  1000   500     300        1.7
#> 4  2000   500     250        6  
#> 5  2000  1000     120        8.3

# expected yearly gain from the higher deductible if you file one claim every k years
claim_every <- c(2, 3, 5, 10)
data.frame(
  claim_every_years = claim_every,
  yearly_gain       = 150 - (1000 - 500) / claim_every
)
#> # A tibble: 4 × 2
#>   claim_every_years yearly_gain
#>               <dbl>       <dbl>
#> 1                 2      -100  
#> 2                 3       -16.7
#> 3                 5        50  
#> 4                10       100


A break even under one year means the higher deductible pays for itself almost at once. A break even of 10 years means the savings are too small to bother.
