def break_even_years(high_deductible, low_deductible, yearly_savings):
    return (high_deductible - low_deductible) / yearly_savings

# $1,000 vs. $500 deductible, saving $150 a year
print(round(break_even_years(high_deductible=1000, low_deductible=500, yearly_savings=150), 2))
#> 3.33

# other quotes you might see

#> $1,000 vs $500, save $50/yr: 10.0 years
#> $1,000 vs $500, save $150/yr: 3.3 years
#> $1,000 vs $500, save $300/yr: 1.7 years
#> $2,000 vs $500, save $250/yr: 6.0 years
#> $2,000 vs $1,000, save $120/yr: 8.3 years

# expected yearly gain from the higher deductible if you file one claim every k years
for k in [2, 3, 5, 10]:
    print(f"claim every {k:>2} years: {150 - (1000 - 500) / k:+.0f} per year")
#> claim every  2 years: -100 per year
#> claim every  3 years: -17 per year
#> claim every  5 years: +50 per year
#> claim every 10 years: +100 per year




Put the higher deductible in B2, the lower deductible in C2, and the yearly savings in D2.
Break even years in E2:
=(B2-C2)/D2
Yearly gain if you file one claim every F2 years:
=D2-(B2-C2)/F2
Copy row 2 down to compare several quotes.



How to read this result: a positive yearly gain means the higher deductible saves money on average. The gain turns negative only if you claim more often than the break even. Either way, pick the higher deductible only if your emergency fund can cover it.

text:
3 Comparing Two Health Plans
A health plan’s real yearly cost is its premiums plus your share of medical bills, minus any money your employer puts in your HSA. Your share can never go above the out of pocket maximum.
Formula: Yearly cost = (Monthly premium × 12) + min(Medical bills, Out of pocket max) − Employer HSA money
This simple version assumes you pay all medical bills up to the out of pocket maximum, so it slightly overstates plans with coinsurance.





Total yearly cost of two health plans in a healthy year and the worst year







Total yearly cost of two health plans in a healthy year and the worst year




Plan A has a $100 monthly premium and a $3,000 out of pocket maximum. Plan B has a $40 monthly premium, a $5,000 out of pocket maximum, and $500 a year from your employer in the HSA. In a healthy year ($300 of care), Plan A costs $1,500 and Plan B costs $280. In the worst year, Plan A costs $4,200 and Plan B costs $4,980.

data.frame(

title: R vs. Python
text:
The sections below are a quick reference for the most important differences in syntax and style between R and Python. Don’t worry about memorizing these right now—just know that they exist, and you’ll see examples of each in the next chapters.





R uses <- (preferred convention) or = for assignment.


Python Uses = for assignment.






x <- 10


x = 10









R Functions are created with function() and assigned to a variable. Function bodies are wrapped in curly braces {}.


Python Functions are defined with the def keyword, followed by a colon and an indented body.






add_fun <- function(a, b) {
  a + b
}


def add_fun(a, b):
    return a + b









R automatically returns the last evaluated expression. The return() function is optional.


Python requires an explicit return statement to return a value—otherwise returns None.






double_fun <- function(x) x * 2


def double_fun(x):
    return x * 2









R has a built-in pipe |> (base R) and the popular %>% operator from magrittr/dplyr for chaining operations.


Python has no native pipe operator. Chaining is done via method calls—polars is especially well-suited for this style.






data |>
  filter(x > 5) |>
  summarise(avg = mean(x))


import polars as pl

(
    data
    .filter(pl.col("x") > 5)
    .select(pl.col("x").mean().alias("avg"))
)









R uses paste(), paste0(), sprintf(), or glue::glue() for string construction.


Python uses f-strings, the .format() method, or % formatting.






name <- "John"
paste0("Hello, ", name)
glue::glue("Hello, {name}")


name = "John"
f"Hello, {name}"









R uses curly braces {} to define code blocks. Indentation is purely stylistic.


Python uses indentation (typically 4 spaces) to define code blocks. Indentation is syntactically required.






if (x > 0) {
  print("positive")
}


if x > 0:
    print("positive")









Spaces, line breaks, and indentation are flexible and stylistic in R


In Python, indentation is syntactic (inconsistent indentation raises an IndentationError). Blank lines are ignored but can be used to separate code blocks for readability.






# R — all of this is valid 
# and produces the same result

# Clean, conventional style
if (x > 0) {
  result <- x * 2
  print(result)
}

# Messy but still valid
if(x>0){result<-x*2
    print(result)}

# Extreme and ugly but works
if   (  x > 0  )    {
result        <-x*2
   print(   result   )
              }


# Python — indentation matters
# Correct: consistent 4-space 
# indentation
if x > 0:
    result = x * 2
    print(result)

# Blank lines are fine 
# they improve readability
def process(x):

    if x > 0:
        result = x * 2

        print(result)

    return result

# Raises IndentationError
if x > 0:
    result = x * 2
        print(result) # ❌ bad indent









R uses 1-based indexing.


Python uses 0-based indexing.






vec <- c("a", "b", "c")
vec[1]   # returns "a"


lst = ["a", "b", "c"]
lst[0]   # returns "a"









R uses NA (with variants like NA_integer_, NA_character_), plus NULL and NaN.


Python uses None natively; polars represents missing values as null in its columnar data structures.






x <- c(1, NA, 3)
is.na(x)


import polars as pl
s = pl.Series([1, None, 3])
s.is_null()









In R, vectors are first-class citizens—most operations are vectorized by default.


In Python, native lists are not vectorized. Vector math requires numpy or columnar libraries like polars.






c(1, 2, 3) * 2   
# returns c(2, 4, 6)


import polars as pl
pl.Series([1, 2, 3]) * 2   
# returns Series [2, 4, 6]









In R, packages are installed with install.packages() and loaded with library().


In Python, packages are installed via pip or conda from the terminal and loaded with import.






install.packages("dplyr")
library(dplyr)


# terminal: pip install polars
import polars as pl









In R, comments are single-line only, using #. No multi-line comment syntax.


In Python, single-line comments use #. Triple-quoted strings ("""...""") are commonly used as block comments or docstrings.






# This is a comment


# This is a comment

"""
This is a multi-line
comment or docstring.
"""









In R, TRUE / FALSE (can be abbreviated as T / F).


In Python, True / False (capitalized, no abbreviation).






flag <- TRUE


flag = True






R uses &, |, ! for vectorized logic; &&, || for scalar logic.
c(TRUE, FALSE) & c(TRUE, TRUE)   # vectorized
TRUE && FALSE                    # scalar
Python uses and, or, not for scalar logic; &, |, ~ for vectorized logic in numpy/polars expressions.
True and False  # scalar

import polars as pl
df.filter((pl.col("a") > 0) & (pl.col("b") < 10)) # vectorized



data.frame is built into base R; enhanced versions include tibble (tidyverse) and data.table.
df <- data.frame(
    name = c("A", "B"), 
    value = c(1, 2)
  )
In Python, data frames are not built-in—requires a library like polars (pl.DataFrame), which offers fast, multithreaded performance and a clean expression API.
import polars as pl
df = pl.DataFrame({"name": ["A", "B"], "value": [1, 2]})
